title: Curvature-Induced Geometric Universality in Non-Hermitian Anderson Transitions
summary: In Euclidean space, universality classes of Anderson transitions are primarily determined by symmetry and spatial dimensionality. Here, we present evidence for a geometry-controlled universality class of non-Hermitian Anderson transitions on hyperbolic-like lattices. In this setting, critical behavior is influenced by the large-scale hyperbolic geometry, characterized by negative curvature, exponential volume growth, and a non-Euclidean notion of spatial scaling. Finite-size scaling of participation ratios across several distinct \( \{p,q\} \) tilings reveals one-parameter scaling collapses with a common critical exponent \( ν\simeq1 \) within numerical accuracy. A complementary phenomenological coarse-grained Landau-Ginzburg analysis shows how exponential correlation-volume growth suppresses critical fluctuations, offering a rationale for the observed mean-field-like scaling. Our results suggest that spatial curvature can act as an additional organizing principle for Anderson-transition universality beyond the conventional dimensionality- and symmetry-based classification.

AI.tldr: The paper provides evidence for a geometry-controlled universality class of non-Hermitian Anderson transitions on hyperbolic-like lattices, where negative curvature and exponential volume growth drive mean-field-like scaling with ν ≃ 1, independent of the specific {p,q} tiling.
AI.motivation: In Euclidean space, universality classes of Anderson transitions are conventionally determined only by symmetry and spatial dimensionality. The authors ask whether spatial geometry itself—specifically hyperbolic (negative-curvature) geometry—can act as an additional organizing principle for critical behavior beyond this standard classification.
AI.method: The study examines non-Hermitian Anderson transitions on hyperbolic-like lattices with negative curvature, exponential volume growth, and non-Euclidean spatial scaling. It performs finite-size scaling of participation ratios across several distinct {p,q} tilings, and complements this with a phenomenological coarse-grained Landau-Ginzburg analysis.
AI.result: Finite-size scaling reveals one-parameter scaling collapses with a common critical exponent ν ≃ 1 across the different {p,q} tilings within numerical accuracy. The coarse-grained Landau-Ginzburg analysis shows that exponential correlation-volume growth suppresses critical fluctuations, providing a rationale for the observed mean-field-like scaling.
AI.conclusion: Spatial curvature can serve as an additional organizing principle for Anderson-transition universality, extending the conventional dimensionality- and symmetry-based classification.

title: Dual-unitary Circuits as a Platform for Quantum Reservoir Computing
summary: Quantum reservoir computing (QRC) is a machine learning approach which employs the internal dynamics of a physical system (the reservoir) to encode and process information. In this work, we explore the use of dual-unitary circuits in a brickwork architecture as a platform for QRC, well suited to current noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices. Dual-unitary circuits present both practical and conceptual advantages. Our results indicate that, under appropriate conditions, dual-unitarity can lead to an enhanced regime of operation: we numerically verify that it improves memory effects and nonlinear processing, and shields against finite-shot noise, mitigating exponential concentration. Moreover, dual unitarity offers an intuitive picture of how operator dynamics gives rise to memory and nonlinear processing in circuit-based reservoirs.

AI.tldr: Dual-unitary brickwork circuits are shown to enhance quantum reservoir computing by improving memory, nonlinear processing, and noise robustness on noisy intermediate-scale quantum hardware.
AI.motivation: Quantum reservoir computing (QRC) exploits a physical system's internal dynamics as a reservoir for encoding and processing information, but practical implementation on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices is limited by decoherence, finite-shot noise, and exponential concentration of information. The paper seeks a reservoir architecture that remains effective under these constraints.
AI.method: The authors investigate dual-unitary circuits arranged in a brickwork architecture as the reservoir substrate. They numerically test this platform, leveraging the property that dual-unitary gates have unitary dynamics also along the time (spatial) direction, which yields exactly solvable operator spreading and provides a controllable setting to examine memory effects, nonlinear processing, and resilience to finite-shot noise.
AI.result: Numerical verification shows that dual-unitarity, under appropriate conditions, enables an enhanced operating regime: it improves memory retention and nonlinear processing capability by the reservoir and shields against finite-shot noise, mitigating exponential concentration.
AI.conclusion: Dual-unitary brickwork circuits are a practically and conceptually advantageous platform for QRC on NISQ devices. Moreover, dual unitarity offers an intuitive framework linking operator dynamics to the emergence of memory and nonlinear processing in circuit-based reservoirs.

title: Finite-energy Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill state-enhanced optical interferometry
summary: We present the case of a Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) state-enhanced optical interferometry with detailed analysis of the phase sensitivity for both the SU(2) and SU(1,1) interferometers. The conventional quantum-enhanced SU(2) interferometer, employing coherent light at one input port and squeezed light at the other, is compared with a modified configuration using coherent light and a GKP state. While it is known that the squeezed vacuum state is the optimal Gaussian resource input mode when paired with the coherent state, we show that the finite-energy GKP state with sufficiently broad envelope outperforms the squeezed vacuum injection, irrespective of the presence of optical losses. This can be attributed to the enhanced robustness coming from the availability of multiple squeezed peaks in the GKP case. However, because lowering the mean photon number reduces the GKP envelope width, the squeezed vacuum input performs better when compared with a GKP state of equal or lower mean photon number. We also observe that optical losses tend to diminish the relative advantage of either input state, since both states approach the (unsqueezed) vacuum state asymptotically. Our work demonstrates the direct application of finite-energy GKP states in optical interferometry along with a methodology for estimating the quantum Fisher information (QFI) and presents a phase estimation procedure using non-Gaussian resources in comparison with conventional Gaussian states.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes a GKP-state-enhanced optical interferometer (SU(2) and SU(1,1)), showing that a finite-energy GKP state with sufficiently broad envelope outperforms squeezed-vacuum injection even with optical loss, though not at equal or lower mean photon number.
AI.motivation: Squeezed vacuum is known to be the optimal Gaussian input when paired with coherent light in SU(2) interferometry. The authors ask whether non-Gaussian resources—specifically finite-energy Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) states—can surpass this Gaussian benchmark for phase sensitivity, and how optical loss and mean photon number affect the comparison.
AI.method: The phase sensitivity of coherent-plus-squeezed-vacuum SU(2) interferometry is compared with a modified configuration using coherent light plus a finite-energy GKP state. A methodology for estimating the quantum Fisher information (QFI) is developed, and a phase estimation procedure is presented using non-Gaussian resources. Both SU(2) and SU(1,1) interferometers are examined, including analysis under optical losses.
AI.result: A finite-energy GKP state with sufficiently broad envelope outperforms squeezed-vacuum injection, irrespective of optical loss, due to enhanced robustness from multiple squeezed peaks. However, since reducing mean photon number narrows the GKP envelope, squeezed vacuum performs better when compared against a GKP state of equal or lower mean photon number. Optical losses diminish the relative advantage of either input state as both asymptotically approach the unsqueezed vacuum.
AI.conclusion: Finite-energy GKP states can be directly applied to optical interferometry and, under suitable conditions, exceed the conventional Gaussian squeezed-vacuum benchmark. The work provides a QFI estimation methodology and a non-Gaussian phase estimation procedure, while clarifying the trade-offs imposed by envelope width, mean photon number, and loss.

title: Reconstructing fluid velocity fields from sparse sensors using a variational quantum algorithm
summary: Reconstructing fields governed by nonlinear partial differential equations (PDEs) from sparse measurements is a challenging task because the governing equations are strongly nonlinear and observations are available at only a few locations. Fluid velocity fields are a representative case. In this paper, we propose a variational quantum algorithm that reconstructs the solution over the entire spacetime domain at once. Rather than marching in time, the method encodes the full discrete spacetime solution in a single variational quantum state, so that all time points are optimized jointly. The cost function combines a sparse-measurement mismatch term with a physics-informed PDE violation term, letting data and the governing equation constrain the solution simultaneously. We demonstrate the method on the one-dimensional Burgers and Kuramoto--Sivashinsky equations using numerical simulations. The results suggest that variational quantum algorithms with a spacetime encoding scheme offer a compact framework for reconstructing nonlinear PDE dynamics.

AI.tldr: A variational quantum algorithm reconstructs nonlinear PDE solutions over the entire spacetime domain at once by encoding the full discrete spacetime solution in a single variational quantum state, jointly optimized via a cost function combining sparse-measurement mismatch and physics-informed PDE violation, demonstrated on 1D Burgers and Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equations.
AI.motivation: Reconstructing fields governed by nonlinear PDEs from sparse measurements is challenging because the governing equations are strongly nonlinear and observations exist at only a few locations; fluid velocity fields are a representative case.
AI.method: A variational quantum algorithm that reconstructs the solution over the entire spacetime domain at once. Instead of marching in time, it encodes the full discrete spacetime solution in a single variational quantum state so all time points are optimized jointly. The cost function combines a sparse-measurement mismatch term with a physics-informed PDE violation term, allowing data and the governing equation to jointly constrain the solution.
AI.result: Demonstrated on the one-dimensional Burgers and Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equations using numerical simulations.
AI.conclusion: Variational quantum algorithms with a spacetime encoding scheme offer a compact framework for reconstructing nonlinear PDE dynamics.

title: The Geometry of Transport in Quantum Walks and Parrondo's Paradox
summary: We study Parrondo's paradox -- the phenomenon where combining losing strategies yields a winning one -- in a minimal discrete-time quantum walk. We introduce the transport vector, encoded in the coin's steady state, whose inner product with the initial coin state gives the walker's asymptotic velocity. More generally, the paradox emerges exactly when the transport vector of the combined strategy falls outside the cone spanned by the individual ones -- a geometric criterion valid for any combination of strategies. It explains, for instance, why composing two coin operators within a single step can produce the paradox while simple alternation between them cannot, since alternation keeps the combined vector confined to the cone. The paradoxical set has nonzero measure, and we compute its probability explicitly in representative cases. This casts the paradox as one instance of designing reachable transport in quantum walks.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes Parrondo's paradox in a minimal discrete-time quantum walk via a "transport vector" encoded in the coin's steady state, whose inner product with the initial coin state yields the walker's asymptotic velocity. The paradox arises exactly when the combined strategy's transport vector lies outside the cone spanned by individual strategies' vectors, a general geometric criterion.
AI.motivation: Parrondo's paradox—combining losing strategies to yield a winning one—is well known in classical settings, but its manifestation and origin in quantum walks lacked a clean, general characterization. The authors aim to identify the precise geometric mechanism underlying the paradox in discrete-time quantum walks.
AI.method: They introduce the transport vector, encoded in the coin's steady state, such that its inner product with the initial coin state gives the asymptotic walker velocity. The paradox is then characterized geometrically: it occurs exactly when the combined strategy's transport vector falls outside the cone spanned by the individual strategies' transport vectors.
AI.result: The geometric criterion explains why composing two coin operators within a single step can produce the paradox, whereas simple alternation between them cannot—since alternation keeps the combined vector confined to the cone. The paradoxical set has nonzero measure, and its probability is computed explicitly in representative cases.
AI.conclusion: Parrondo's paradox in quantum walks is recast as one instance of designing reachable transport, providing a general geometric framework applicable to arbitrary combinations of strategies.

title: Python in the front, party in the Backline: compiling quantum workloads across CPUs, GPUs, and FPGAs
summary: Moving from quantum research and development to production-grade, fault-tolerant quantum workload execution remains one of the most significant challenges facing quantum platform builders. While Python frameworks have enabled an easy entry point for quantum algorithm design, the low-latency requirements for real-time quantum error correction (QEC) demand performance that traditional interpreted environments cannot provide. FPGAs and ASICs play a central role at these layers, but their specialized programming models make development rigid and time-consuming. CPUs, GPUs, and other accelerators introduce a different challenge: as infrastructure becomes increasingly heterogeneous, programming across different devices and their associated abstractions becomes more complex. Allowing researchers to write workloads in high-level languages that map to low-latency execution across diverse distributed target platforms will enable the development of key infrastructure for utility-scale quantum systems. For this, we introduce $\textit{Backline}$, a heterogeneous compilation and runtime framework built within PennyLane and Catalyst. Backline allows us to design and build quantum-classical workloads for high-performance and low-latency devices, with compilation directly from a Python interface through MLIR. We demonstrate the compilation and execution of several quantum workloads with low-latency data movement across a mix of CPUs, GPUs, and FPGAs, for both local and distributed remote hardware targets, all from a vendor-agnostic Python frontend. With an AMD VPK120 FPGA board as the controller, issuing each round from its hardware-handshake engine, we measured median steady-state round-trip latencies over RoCE v2 of $2.305~μ$s to an AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO CPU and $4.5~μ$s to an AMD Instinct MI210 GPU across $10^6-1$ rounds per path, demonstrating microsecond-scale synchronous co-processing.

AI.tldr: Backline is a heterogeneous compilation and runtime framework within PennyLane/Catalyst that compiles vendor-agnostic Python quantum-classical workloads directly to low-latency hardware (CPUs, GPUs, FPGAs) via MLIR, achieving microsecond-scale synchronized co-processing.
AI.motivation: Scaling quantum systems from R&D to production-grade fault-tolerant execution is a major challenge. Real-time QEC demands low latency that interpreted Python environments cannot deliver. FPGAs/ASICs offer needed performance but have rigid, time-consuming programming models, while increasing hardware heterogeneity (CPUs, GPUs, accelerators) complicates cross-device programming. A high-level, vendor-agnostic path to low-latency execution across diverse distributed targets is needed.
AI.method: Backline is a heterogeneous compilation and runtime framework built within PennyLane and Catalyst. It enables design and construction of quantum-classical workloads for high-performance, low-latency devices, compiling directly from a Python interface through MLIR, targeting a mix of CPUs, GPUs, and FPGAs across local and distributed remote hardware.
AI.result: Using an AMD VPK120 FPGA board as the controller issuing rounds from its hardware-handshake engine, median steady-state round-trip latencies over RoCE v2 were measured at 2.305 μs to an AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO CPU and 4.5 μs to an AMD Instinct MI210 GPU, across 10^6−1 rounds per path, demonstrating microsecond-scale synchronous co-processing.
AI.conclusion: Backline provides a vendor-agnostic Python frontend for compiling and executing quantum-classical workloads with low-latency data movement across heterogeneous distributed targets, delivering microsecond-scale synchronous co-processing key to utility-scale quantum infrastructure.

title: Universal Entanglement Dynamics of Unitary Operators
summary: The entangling power of a unitary operator acting on a bipartite Hilbert space measures the entanglement it generates from product states, averaged over the inputs. A finite-dimensional unitary has a spectral decomposition $U=\sum_{a=1}^{n}e^{iθ_a}P_a$, where $e^{iθ_a}$ are the eigenvalues, $P_a$ the corresponding eigen-projectors, and $n$ is the number of distinct eigenvalues. After removing an overall phase, the entangling power is a function on the $(n-1)$-torus of relative eigenphases at fixed spectral projectors. We prove that this function is stationary at all $2^{n-1}$ points on the torus where every relative phase is $0$ or $π$, which we define as \textit{corners}. Up to an overall phase, $U$ at each corner is a generalized reflection $R=\mathbb{I}-2Q$ satisfying $R^2=\mathbb{I}$, where $Q$ is the sum of spectral projectors whose relative phase is $π$. At the corner the entangling power is expressed in terms of seven local-unitary invariants of $Q$. A unitary gate $U$ can be realized as a corner of some projector family if and only if $U^2\propto\mathbb{I}$, a condition satisfied by many Clifford and non-Clifford gates. We illustrate the theorem with two-qubit gates, $SU(N)$ channel decompositions, and two-site spin chains, obtaining examples of minima, maxima, and saddle points. In addition, a corner that is a saddle point on the full phase torus can appear as a local maximum or minimum along different time-evolution trajectories.

AI.tldr: The entangling power of a unitary is a function on the torus of relative eigenphases; it is stationary at all "corner" points where each relative phase is 0 or π, corresponding to generalized reflections, with the value expressed via seven invariants of a projector.
AI.motivation: The entangling power quantifies entanglement generated by a unitary from product states. Understanding where this quantity is stationary and how it depends on spectral data is important for characterizing and engineering entangling gates, yet a systematic account of its critical points in terms of the unitary's spectrum was lacking.
AI.method: Spectral decomposition of a finite-dimensional unitary on a bipartite Hilbert space, with the overall phase removed so entangling power becomes a function on the (n−1)-torus of relative eigenphases at fixed spectral projectors. Analyze stationarity at the 2^{n−1} corner points where each relative phase is 0 or π; show the unitary is then a generalized reflection R = I − 2Q and express entangling power in seven local-unitary invariants of Q. Derive the realizability condition U² ∝ I, then illustrate with two-qubit gates, SU(N) channel decompositions, and two-site spin chains.
AI.result: All 2^{n−1} corner points are stationary points of the entangling power. At each corner the unitary is a generalized reflection and the entangling power is given by seven local-unitary invariants of the projector Q. A gate U is a corner of some projector family iff U² ∝ I, a condition met by many Clifford and non-Clifford gates. Examples yield minima, maxima, and saddle points. A corner that is a saddle on the full phase torus can act as a local maximum or minimum along different time-evolution trajectories.
AI.conclusion: The entangling power's critical structure is governed by corner points of the relative-phase torus, universally stationary, tied to generalized reflections, and characterized by seven projector invariants; the U² ∝ I criterion identifies realizable corner gates and the findings connect to gate design, channel decompositions, and spin-chain dynamics.

title: Spectral Core-Tail Architecture for Locally Certified Gibbs-State Preparation
summary: Preparing a quantum Gibbs state requires reproducing both its thermal distribution and the associated many-body eigenspaces. In this work, we formalize the spectral core-tail architecture (SCTA) as a framework comprising a structured thermal core, a geometrically characterized unitary tail, and an exact residual measuring the remaining core-frame Hamiltonian mismatch. We derive a local Gibbs-state error bound separating core-preparation, tail-implementation, and modeling errors. The modeling contribution is volume uniform when its Kubo-Mori response meets the shell summability condition and the relevant local data remain uniform. We then highlight three anchor Hamiltonian classes which admit exact core-tail constructions with zero residuals. For small deformations of an exact anchor, we employ a Schrieffer-Wolff reduction procedure to construct a corrected core-tail pair that formally removes the deformation order by order. Under uniform locality and solvability assumptions, we show that the first-order reduction yields a residual that remains bounded and is quadratic in the deformation strength. Furthermore, we numerically test the first-order reduction on deformed graph-stabilizer Hamiltonians. The numerical results show approximately quadratic suppression of both the Hamiltonian-level mismatch and the local Gibbs-state error in the perturbative regime. We also find that the constructed correction circuit structure remains useful as a variational ansatz beyond perturbative control, often improving on both the bare and prescribed first-order states.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes a spectral core-tail architecture (SCTA) for preparing quantum Gibbs states, dividing the problem into a thermal core, a unitary tail, and an exact residual. It derives a local error bound and a volume-uniform modeling bound, identifies three anchor Hamiltonian classes with exact zero-residual constructions, and applies a Schrieffer-Wolff reduction to handle small deformations with quadratically bounded residuals, validated numerically on deformed graph-stabilizer Hamiltonians.
AI.motivation: Preparing a quantum Gibbs state requires reproducing both the thermal distribution and the associated many-body eigenspaces. Existing approaches lack a unified framework that cleanly separates thermal preparation, unitary basis implementation, and modeling error, especially with controllable locality and volume-uniform error bounds under perturbations.
AI.method: The authors formalize the spectral core-tail architecture (SCTA): a structured thermal core, a geometrically characterized unitary tail, and an exact residual measuring core-frame Hamiltonian mismatch. They derive a local Gibbs-state error bound separating core-preparation, tail-implementation, and modeling errors, with volume uniformity under a Kubo-Mori shell summability condition. They identify three anchor Hamiltonian classes with exact core-tail constructions (zero residual) and use a Schrieffer-Wolff reduction to build corrected core-tail pairs for small deformations. They numerically test first-order reduction on deformed graph-stabilizer Hamiltonians.
AI.result: The modeling contribution is volume uniform when the Kubo-Mori response satisfies shell summability and local data remain uniform. Under uniform locality and solvability assumptions, the first-order reduction yields a residual that remains bounded and is quadratic in the deformation strength. Numerics on deformed graph-stabilizer Hamiltonians show approximately quadratic suppression of both Hamiltonian-level mismatch and local Gibbs-state error in the perturbative regime, and the correction circuit remains useful as a variational ansatz beyond perturbative control, often improving on both bare and prescribed first-order states.
AI.conclusion: SCTA provides a principled separation of Gibbs-state preparation into core, tail, and residual components with rigorous, volume-uniform error control. Schrieffer-Wolff reduction extends exact anchors to weakly deformed Hamiltonians with quadratic residual scaling, and the correction circuit has practical variational value beyond the perturbative regime.

title: Bell tests for collider decay processes
summary: We propose Bell tests for collider decays using independently sampled analysis axes as settings and detector regions to assign binary or null outcomes. We show that a Bell violation requires postselection, opening a loophole. However, under measurement independence and operational equivalence of acceptance events across settings, any local model exploiting the loophole must be nonclassical in the sense of measurement contextuality. We derive a Bell inequality violated by singlet correlations when the effective spin-analyzing powers are sufficiently high. Its violation then witnesses Bell nonlocality or measurement contextuality.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Bell tests for collider decays using independently sampled analysis axes as measurement settings and detector regions for outcomes, showing that Bell violation requires postselection (a loophole), but that any local model exploiting it must be measurement-contextual; a derived Bell inequality, violated by singlet correlations at high analyzing power, witnesses either Bell nonlocality or contextuality.
AI.motivation: Extending Bell tests to high-energy collider decays faces practical constraints, notably the need to handle imperfect detection and postselection. The paper aims to establish what can rigorously be concluded about nonclassicality in such collider settings despite these limitations.
AI.method: The authors construct Bell tests for collider decays, using independently sampled analysis axes as settings and detector regions to assign binary or null outcomes. They assume measurement independence and operational equivalence of acceptance events across settings, and derive a Bell inequality satisfied by local models, examining the effect of postselection on the loophole.
AI.result: Bell violation in this scheme requires postselection, which opens a loophole. Under the stated assumptions, any local model that exploits the postselection loophole must be nonclassical in the sense of measurement contextuality. The derived Bell inequality is violated by singlet correlations when the effective spin-analyzing powers are sufficiently high.
AI.conclusion: Violation of the derived inequality witnesses either Bell nonlocality or measurement contextuality, so collider decay experiments can certify nonclassicality even when postselection is unavoidable, provided analyzing powers are high enough.

title: Multivariate quantum state preparation with optimized tensor networks
summary: Quantics tensor trains are attracting intense interest for quantum-inspired computing and quantum state preparation. These methods, which approximate continuum functions by representing their amplitude encoding as a matrix product state (MPS), are exceedingly powerful for univariate functions but rapidly become challenging when handling multivariate functions, since the linear chain topology leads to a large distance between highly-entangled qubits. We overcome this limitation by introducing SCENT (Spectral Clustering for Entanglement miNimizing Trees). SCENT is a protocol that utilizes efficiently-computable pairwise entanglement metrics to determine a suitable tree tensor network (TTN) structure, which can then be efficiently approximated using tensor cross-interpolation (TCI); we find that it substantially outperforms MPS methods and improves upon previous TTN methods. We then apply these optimized TTNs to state preparation, introducing an approximate circuit compilation method based on environment-tensor methods without significantly conceding overall accuracy. Importantly, the inherent gauge freedom of TTNs can be directly exploited in this method, resulting in higher fidelity at a given circuit depth. We demonstrate this quantum state-preparation pipeline on archetypal state-preparation problems in quantum chemistry and financial portfolio optimization. In our flagship demonstration, we encode a 20-variable probability distribution with long-ranged, non-nearest neighbor inter-variable correlations in a 200-qubit state-preparation circuit with infidelity $7.44\times 10^{-9}$ using only 43284 CNOTs; depth and fidelity can be traded, allowing the same distribution to be prepared to infidelity $10^{-3}$ with as few as 5584 CNOTs.

AI.tldr: SCENT uses pairwise entanglement metrics to build tree tensor network structures that outperform MPS for multivariate functions, enabling efficient quantum state preparation with high fidelity at low circuit depth.
AI.motivation: Quantics tensor trains are powerful for univariate functions but struggle with multivariate functions because the linear MPS chain topology places highly-entangled qubits far apart, making approximation inefficient.
AI.method: SCENT (Spectral Clustering for Entanglement miNimizing Trees) uses efficiently-computable pairwise entanglement metrics to determine a suitable TTN structure, approximated via tensor cross-interpolation (TCI). Optimized TTNs are applied to state preparation via an approximate circuit compilation method based on environment-tensor methods, exploiting TTN gauge freedom for higher fidelity at fixed circuit depth.
AI.result: Demonstrated on quantum chemistry and financial portfolio optimization state-preparation problems. Flagship: a 20-variable probability distribution with long-ranged, non-nearest-neighbor correlations encoded in a 200-qubit circuit with infidelity 7.44e-9 using 43284 CNOTs; the same distribution can be prepared to infidelity 1e-3 with as few as 5584 CNOTs.
AI.conclusion: SCENT substantially outperforms MPS methods and improves on previous TTN methods, offering a flexible depth-fidelity trade-off for quantum state preparation.

title: Execution-transcript privacy for fault-tolerant surface-code memories
summary: A fault-tolerant quantum computer runs behind a telemetry stream logging syndromes, decoder actions, resets and timing separately from the answer. Can it reveal the logical input? For a distance-$d$ rotated surface-code memory on a fixed schedule of $T=Θ(d)$ rounds, under three stated hypotheses (sector-scalar honest backbone, transcript locality, Kotecky-Preiss smallness), the channel from logical qubit to transcript is $e^{-Θ(d)}$-close in diamond norm to one that ignores the input. A statement of this kind follows generically from correctability-privacy duality. Anisotropy does not. Each logical axis pays the distance of its own coset, so under amplitude damping the computational-basis label is governed by the code's $Z$-distance $d_Z\ge d_{\min}$ and not by the code distance. Two codes of quantum distance $1$ make the gap concrete. A phase-flip code's $X$-syndrome transcript is exactly input-independent under unobserved damping, while a repetition code leaks at first order. A matched converse identifies the records that do expose it, among them a lattice-surgery parity readout. On a 156-qubit superconducting processor our sufficient certificate misses by $21.5\times$, so the theorem cannot be invoked there. Measured directly, a $d_Z=1$ memory's record identifies its input with total variation $\ge 0.927$ under randomised, label-balanced acquisition. Holding the code fixed and varying the damping exposure reproduces the parameter-free law, with exponent $0.85\pm0.03$ against a predicted $0.86$. Randomized encoding returns the statistic to the floor at no two-qubit-gate cost. Fault tolerance does not grant transcript privacy. It relocates it, and only to the logical state, not to the circuit's identity.

AI.tldr: Under stated hypotheses, the logical-qubit-to-telemetry-transcript channel of a distance-d rotated surface-code memory is e^{-Θ(d)}-close in diamond norm to an input-independent channel, but this privacy applies only to the logical state, not the circuit's identity.
AI.motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computers emit telemetry (syndromes, decoder actions, resets, timing) separately from logical answers. The paper asks whether such a transcript can leak the logical input, and whether fault tolerance itself guarantees transcript privacy.
AI.method: Analyzes the channel from logical qubit to transcript for a distance-d rotated surface-code memory on a fixed T=Θ(d) round schedule, under three hypotheses: sector-scalar honest backbone, transcript locality, and Kotecky-Preiss smallness. Uses correctability-privacy duality generically, plus a matched converse to identify records that expose the input.
AI.result: The channel is e^{-Θ(d)}-close in diamond norm to an input-ignoring channel. Anisotropy breaks the generic statement: each logical axis pays its own coset distance, so under amplitude damping the computational-basis label is governed by Z-distance d_Z ≥ d_min, not the code distance. A phase-flip code's X-syndrome transcript is exactly input-independent under unobserved damping, while a repetition code leaks at first order. On a 156-qubit superconducting processor the sufficient certificate misses by 21.5×, so the theorem cannot be invoked; a d_Z=1 memory's record identifies its input with total variation ≥ 0.927 under randomised, label-balanced acquisition. Varying damping exposure reproduces the parameter-free law with exponent 0.85±0.03 against a predicted 0.86.
AI.conclusion: Fault tolerance does not grant transcript privacy; it relocates privacy, and only to the logical state, not to the circuit's identity. Randomized encoding returns the statistic to the floor at no two-qubit-gate cost.

title: Certified measurement and control of an entanglement-breaking index on programmable hardware
comment: 14 pages, 4 tables. Ancillary files contain machine-readable interval certificates, the gated search and certification code, the schedule engine, and the float64 atlases
summary: The entanglement-breaking index of a quantum channel, the number of self-compositions after which the channel destroys all entanglement with any reference, has to our knowledge never been measured. We show that a certified thermal collision feedback loop makes this integer both measurable and controllable on current programmable hardware, every load-bearing quantity delivered as an interval-arithmetic certificate. On the measurement side: a target list for the integer staircase n_EB(p) with decision-point negativities certified at margins 0.025 to 0.109; an exact per-round depolarising model in which the selected staircase survives realistic noise as certified integers; an exact, tight compilation of the round unitary (seven CNOTs all-to-all, five native arbitrary-angle gates, ten on heavy-hex); and a 33-million-draw gated search bounding the thermal valley's contrast by a wall with an interior maximum, a certified 2.85x10^-3 near floor 89. On the control side: the model composes rounds of differing bath polarisation exactly, so the valley becomes a pulsed valve, switching at a certified minimal pulse of exactly eight rounds; the optimal pulsed signal, a certified 3.43x10^-3, beats the static protocol, so the best valley measurement is intrinsically pulsed; and a coherent tilt of the bath Bloch vector lifts the signal to a certified 8.6x10^-3, three times the static ceiling, at zero population cost. Valley signatures certifiably die near per-round noise strength 10^-4, fixing the error-extrapolation burden. The staircase is a near-term experiment; the pulsed valley a precisely priced one.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that the entanglement-breaking index of a quantum channel—previously never measured—can be both measured and controlled on current programmable hardware using a certified thermal collision feedback loop, with all key quantities expressed as interval-arithmetic certificates.
AI.motivation: The entanglement-breaking index (the number of self-compositions after which a channel destroys all entanglement with any reference) had never been experimentally measured. The authors aim to make this integer measurable and controllable on existing quantum hardware.
AI.method: A certified thermal collision feedback loop is used. Methods include: a target list for the integer staircase n_EB(p) with certified decision-point negativities; an exact per-round depolarising model preserving the staircase under realistic noise; a tight compilation of the round unitary (seven CNOTs all-to-all, five native arbitrary-angle gates, ten on heavy-hex); a 33-million-draw gated search bounding the thermal valley's contrast; exact composition of rounds with differing bath polarisation for control; and a coherent tilt of the bath Bloch vector to boost signal.
AI.result: Decision-point negativities certified at margins 0.025 to 0.109. The thermal valley has an interior maximum certified at 2.85x10^-3 near floor 89. Control results: switching at a certified minimal pulse of eight rounds; optimal pulsed signal of 3.43x10^-3 beating the static protocol; coherent bath tilt lifts signal to 8.6x10^-3 (three times the static ceiling) at zero population cost. Valley signatures vanish near per-round noise strength 10^-4.
AI.conclusion: The entanglement-breaking staircase is feasible as a near-term experiment, while the pulsed thermal valley is precisely priced. The best valley measurement is intrinsically pulsed, and the error-extrapolation burden is fixed by the noise threshold at 10^-4.

title: From the Unknown to the Desired: Transforming Unknown Initial States in the Resource Theory of Work and Heat
summary: We study thermodynamic state transformations in the resource theory of work and heat when the initial quantum state is unknown. Moving beyond state-dependent protocols, we develop a universal framework in which a single transformation applies to all admissible input states. For mutually commuting conserved charges, we construct charge-conserving protocols whose transformation error, quantified by trace distance, decays super-polynomially with the number of system copies. As an application, we demonstrate universal work extraction: asymptotically optimal work can be extracted without microscopic knowledge of the initial state, with a super-polynomially small error. Our results show that thermodynamic state transformations remain achievable under limited prior information and establish a universal framework for resource-theoretic thermodynamics beyond the state-aware setting.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a universal framework for thermodynamic state transformations in the resource theory of work and heat when the initial quantum state is unknown, showing that transformation error decays super-polynomially with the number of copies for commuting conserved charges.
AI.motivation: Standard thermodynamic protocols are state-dependent, requiring microscopic knowledge of the initial state. This raises the question of whether thermodynamic transformations remain achievable when prior information about the initial quantum state is limited or unavailable.
AI.method: The authors move beyond state-dependent protocols by constructing a universal framework in which a single transformation applies to all admissible input states. For mutually commuting conserved charges, they build charge-conserving protocols and quantify transformation error via trace distance as a function of the number of system copies.
AI.result: The transformation error, measured by trace distance, decays super-polynomially with the number of system copies. As an application, universal work extraction achieves asymptotically optimal work without microscopic knowledge of the initial state, with super-polynomially small error.
AI.conclusion: Thermodynamic state transformations remain achievable under limited prior information, establishing a universal framework for resource-theoretic thermodynamics beyond the state-aware setting.

title: Materials for Quantum Information Science: Roles in the Quantum Evolution 2.0
summary: Quantum information science is entering a second phase, the Quantum Evolution 2.0, in which the challenge has shifted from demonstrating coherent control of individual quantum states to building scalable multi-qubit processors and networks. This transition places materials science at the center of the field. Across superconducting circuits, quantum defects, quantum photonic devices, and emerging materials platforms, including two-dimensional materials and heterostructures, performance is now limited less by device design than by poorly controlled surfaces, buried interfaces, and defects whose atomic identities remain incompletely known. This review surveys the materials challenges of these quantum platforms together with the characterization methods needed to resolve them. For each platform we identify the dominant decoherence mechanisms, the current state of materials understanding, and the most pressing open materials problems. A cross-platform comparison then reveals a shared structure-coherence problem. The implicated material chemistry recurs across platforms, involving light elements in disordered or buried environments, yet no platform can quantitatively connect a specific atomic-scale structure to a measured change in coherence. We close by identifying three needs, mechanistic understanding of decoherence at the atomistic level, high-throughput proxy metrics predictive of device performance, and characterization tools built for quantum materials, whose resolution would advance coherence, scalability, and integration across all platforms.

AI.tldr: This review argues that as quantum information science moves to scalable multi-qubit processors ("Quantum Evolution 2.0"), materials science becomes the central bottleneck; surfaces, interfaces, and unidentified defects—not device design—limit coherence across superconducting, defect, photonic, 2D, and heterostructure platforms.
AI.motivation: The field's challenge has shifted from coherent control of individual quantum states to scalable multi-qubit processors and networks, making materials the limiting factor. Performance is constrained by poorly controlled surfaces, buried interfaces, and defects with incompletely known atomic identities, so a materials-centric synthesis is needed.
AI.method: A cross-platform review: for superconducting circuits, quantum defects, quantum photonic devices, and emerging platforms (2D materials and heterostructures), the authors survey dominant decoherence mechanisms, the state of materials understanding, and pressing open materials problems, then perform a cross-platform comparison of the shared structure-coherence problem and the characterization methods needed.
AI.result: A shared structure-coherence problem emerges across platforms: the implicated material chemistry recurs and involves light elements in disordered or buried environments, yet no platform can quantitatively link a specific atomic-scale structure to a measured change in coherence.
AI.conclusion: Three needs are identified: atomistic mechanistic understanding of decoherence, high-throughput proxy metrics predictive of device performance, and characterization tools built for quantum materials; resolving them would advance coherence, scalability, and integration across all platforms.

title: Non-Multiplicativity of the Holevo Barycenter of Quantum Channels
summary: The Holevo barycenter of a quantum channel is the unique output state obtained as the average output of any ensemble achieving the Holevo capacity. Given two quantum channels, the multiplicativity problem asks whether this barycenter tensorizes under parallel composition, namely whether the barycenter of the product channel coincides with the tensor product of the individual barycenters. This question is closely related to the additivity problem for the Holevo capacity: additivity implies tensorization of the Holevo barycenter, while tensorization alone is not sufficient for additivity. Although a construction is known that demonstrates the existence of channels with non-additive Holevo capacity, their corresponding Holevo barycenters still tensorize, leaving open whether multiplicativity might ultimately hold universally. Here, we answer this question in the negative by exhibiting channels for which the Holevo barycenter is not multiplicative under the tensor product of the channel with itself. Moreover, we show that the entropy of the Holevo barycenter is neither universally subadditive nor universally superadditive under tensor product.

AI.tldr: The Holevo barycenter of a quantum channel need not tensorize: explicit channels are constructed whose Holevo barycenter is not multiplicative under the tensor product of the channel with itself, and the barycenter entropy is shown to be neither universally subadditive nor superadditive.
AI.motivation: The multiplicativity of the Holevo barycenter under parallel composition is linked to the additivity problem for Holevo capacity. Additivity implies tensorization of the barycenter, but tensorization alone does not imply additivity. Known constructions of channels with non-additive Holevo capacity still have tensorizing barycenters, so it remained open whether multiplicativity might hold universally. This work aims to settle that question.
AI.method: The authors construct explicit quantum channels and analyze the behavior of the Holevo barycenter—the unique average output state from any ensemble achieving Holevo capacity—under the tensor product of the channel with itself.
AI.result: Channels are exhibited for which the Holevo barycenter is not multiplicative under the tensor product of the channel with itself. Additionally, the entropy of the Holevo barycenter is shown to be neither universally subadditive nor universally superadditive under tensor product.
AI.conclusion: Multiplicativity of the Holevo barycenter does not hold universally, answering the open question in the negative. The link between barycenter tensorization and Holevo capacity additivity is therefore not strong enough to force universal multiplicativity.

title: Balancing Expressivity and Overfitting in Quantum Gaussian Process Regression
summary: Active learning is a paradigm of machine learning that can be utilized to model expensive black-box functions by training a surrogate model from actively queried training points. The performance of this framework depends heavily on the choice of the surrogate model. When the surrogate is Gaussian Process Regression (GPR), its performance is largely determined by the expressivity of the underlying kernel. In this work, we investigate the peculiarities of using a quantum kernel to change the computational dynamics of active learning with GPR, focusing on the sensitivity to regularization by hyperparameter tuning. While generic, unstructured kernels suffer from exponential concentration at large scale, we empirically demonstrate that even at small scale overfitting can collapse GPR performance. Kernel regularization can be used to counteract this effect, but due to the smoothness of the quantum fidelity kernel, regularization must be carefully chosen to balance expressivity and overfitting. Our qualitative results transfer to the practical application of restricted quantum kernels designed to avoid exponential concentration and also present the kinds of noise that may be valuable to kernel training in near-term quantum devices.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how using quantum kernels in Gaussian Process Regression active learning affects model performance, showing that regularization via hyperparameter tuning is critical because the smooth quantum fidelity kernel can easily overfit even at small scale.
AI.motivation: Active learning with GPR relies heavily on the surrogate model's kernel expressivity. While generic unstructured kernels suffer from exponential concentration at large scale, the sensitivity of quantum-kernel-based GPR to regularization and overfitting remains underexplored.
AI.method: Empirically investigate quantum kernels within GPR-based active learning, focusing on sensitivity to regularization through hyperparameter tuning; analyze computational dynamics, overfitting effects, and the smoothness properties of the quantum fidelity kernel.
AI.result: Even at small scale, overfitting can collapse GPR performance. Kernel regularization counteracts this, but due to the smoothness of the quantum fidelity kernel, regularization must be carefully tuned to balance expressivity and overfitting. Findings transfer to restricted quantum kernels designed to avoid exponential concentration, and certain near-term device noises may benefit kernel training.
AI.conclusion: Careful regularization is essential when using quantum kernels in GPR active learning; the trade-off between expressivity and overfitting is central, and results extend to practical restricted kernels and noisy near-term quantum settings.

title: Induced random mixed states are symmetric Dirichlet mixtures
summary: We establish an exact equivalence in distribution between $D$-dimensional random mixed states induced by partial traces over $K$-dimensional environments and the Mai-Alquier distribution, a mixture of $K$ independent Haar-random pure states weighted by a symmetric Dirichlet distribution. This identification recasts a class of expectation values for induced ensembles into calculations involving Dirichlet moments and low-order Haar averages on a single-system state space. As applications, we recover exact purity moments up to fourth order, derive the mean Hilbert--Schmidt distance between independent induced ensembles with possibly different environment dimensions, and obtain exact average determinants. These results provide a unified and constructive perspective on induced random mixed states and on the evaluation of quantities such as purity moments, overlaps, and determinants.

AI.tldr: The paper proves an exact distributional equivalence between D-dimensional random mixed states from partial traces over K-dimensional environments and the Mai-Alquier distribution (a Dirichlet-weighted mixture of K Haar-random pure states), then uses this to compute purity moments, Hilbert-Schmidt distances, and average determinants in closed form.
AI.motivation: Induced random mixed states (partial traces over environments) are central to quantum information, yet computing their expectation values—such as purity moments, overlaps, and determinants—typically requires heavy machinery. The paper seeks a unified, constructive framework that simplifies these calculations.
AI.method: The authors establish an exact equivalence in distribution between induced ensembles from partial traces over K-dimensional environments and the Mai-Alquier distribution, a mixture of K independent Haar-random pure states weighted by a symmetric Dirichlet distribution. This recasts expectation values into Dirichlet moments combined with low-order Haar averages on a single-system space.
AI.result: The equivalence yields exact purity moments up to fourth order, the mean Hilbert-Schmidt distance between independent induced ensembles with possibly differing environment dimensions, and exact average determinants.
AI.conclusion: The identification provides a unified and constructive perspective on induced random mixed states and on evaluating quantities such as purity moments, overlaps, and determinants.

title: Josephson energy of superconducting junctions: amorphous versus crystalline tunnel barriers
summary: The Josephson energy $E_J$ is a key parameter governing the properties of transmon superconducting qubits. In Al/AlO$_x$/Al junctions, $E_J$ is set by electron tunneling through an ultrathin oxide barrier and therefore depends exponentially on the atomic structure of the barrier. We compute $E_J$ by first-principles device modeling based on the NEGF-DFT quantum-transport method, comparing a junction with a crystalline Al$_2$O$_3$ barrier against ten junctions with melt--quenched amorphous Al$_2$O$_3$ barriers of the same thickness. From the Fermi-level transmission and the Ambegaokar--Baratoff relation, we obtain a mean $E_J/h$ of $2.78$ GHz for the amorphous ensemble, with a standard deviation of $4.67$ GHz, compared with $0.73$ GHz for the crystalline reference; individual amorphous values span nearly two orders of magnitude. Scattering-state analysis shows that transport is quantum tunneling and that the variability originates from stoichiometric inhomogeneity of the amorphous oxide: Al-rich, low-barrier regions can connect into percolation-like tunneling pathways that strongly enhance the conductance. A realistic $200\times200$ nm$^2$ junction self-averages over more than $2\times10^4$ such microscopic regions. These results establish a quantitative atomistic route from oxide microstructure to the superconducting-circuit energy scale $E_J$.

AI.tldr: First-principles NEGF-DFT modeling of Al/AlO$_x$/Al Josephson junctions shows that amorphous Al$_2$O$_3$ barriers yield a mean $E_J/h$ of 2.78 GHz with a 4.67 GHz standard deviation (vs. 0.73 GHz for crystalline), with variability arising from stoichiometric inhomogeneity and percolation-like tunneling pathways; a realistic 200×200 nm$^2$ junction self-averages over >2×10$^4$ microscopic regions.
AI.motivation: The Josephson energy $E_J$ governs transmon qubit properties. In Al/AlO$_x$/Al junctions, $E_J$ depends exponentially on the atomic structure of the ultrathin oxide barrier via electron tunneling, so an atomistic understanding linking oxide microstructure to $E_J$ is needed.
AI.method: First-principles device modeling using the NEGF-DFT quantum-transport method. One junction with a crystalline Al$_2$O$_3$ barrier is compared against ten melt-quenched amorphous Al$_2$O$_3$ barriers of identical thickness. $E_J$ is derived from Fermi-level transmission combined with the Ambegaokar--Baratoff relation, and scattering-state analysis is used to characterize the transport mechanism.
AI.result: Amorphous ensemble: mean $E_J/h = 2.78$ GHz with standard deviation of 4.67 GHz; crystalline reference: 0.73 GHz. Individual amorphous values span nearly two orders of magnitude. Transport is confirmed as quantum tunneling. Variability originates from stoichiometric inhomogeneity—Al-rich, low-barrier regions forming percolation-like tunneling pathways that strongly enhance conductance. A realistic 200×200 nm$^2$ junction self-averages over more than $2\times10^4$ microscopic regions.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a quantitative atomistic route connecting oxide microstructure to the superconducting-circuit energy scale $E_J$, highlighting the impact of amorphous barrier inhomogeneity on transmon qubit parameters.

title: A Block Tensor Train Burer-Monteiro Framework for Low-Rank Quantum State Tomography
summary: Quantum state tomography is a fundamental technique for estimating the state of a quantum system from measured data and plays a crucial role in evaluating the performance of quantum devices. However, standard estimation methods become computationally prohibitive as the system size increases due to the exponential growth of the density matrix, describing a quantum state, with the number of qubits. We propose a low-rank tensor-network framework for mixed-state quantum state tomography based on a block tensor train (Block-TT) factorization. Specifically, the density matrix is represented as the contraction of a Block-TT with its Hermitian transpose, yielding a TT analogue of the Burer-Monteiro factorization. This parameterization guarantees Hermiticity and positive semidefiniteness by construction while compressing the number of optimization variables from exponential to linear in the number of qubits. Building on this representation, we develop single-site and two-site density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) algorithms for estimating quantum states from compressed measurements. The resulting methods operate directly on the compressed parameterization, support adaptive rank refinement, and exploit efficient tensor-network contractions for expectation-value evaluation. The framework is applicable to a broad class of low-rank quantum states, including pure states, nearly pure states, and ground states that admit accurate tensor-network approximations. Numerical experiments demonstrate accurate state reconstruction from limited measurements together with substantial reductions in memory requirements and computational cost compared with conventional low-rank tomography methods.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a low-rank tensor-network framework for mixed-state quantum state tomography using a block tensor train (Block-TT) factorization of the density matrix, with DMRG-based algorithms that reduce optimization variables from exponential to linear in qubit number.
AI.motivation: Standard quantum state tomography becomes computationally prohibitive as system size grows, because the density matrix dimension grows exponentially with the number of qubits. Existing low-rank tomography methods still incur high memory and computational costs, so a more scalable parameterization is needed.
AI.method: The density matrix is represented as the contraction of a Block-TT with its Hermitian transpose, forming a TT analogue of the Burer-Monteiro factorization. This construction enforces Hermiticity and positive semidefiniteness by design and compresses optimization variables to linear scaling in qubit count. Single-site and two-site DMRG algorithms are developed to estimate states from compressed measurements, operating directly on the compressed parameterization, supporting adaptive rank refinement, and using efficient tensor-network contractions for expectation-value evaluation.
AI.result: Numerical experiments show accurate state reconstruction from limited measurements, with substantial reductions in memory requirements and computational cost compared to conventional low-rank tomography methods.
AI.conclusion: The Block-TT-based framework is broadly applicable to low-rank quantum states such as pure, nearly pure, and ground states admitting accurate tensor-network approximations, offering a scalable and efficient approach to mixed-state quantum state tomography.

title: Noise Limits on Fault-Tolerant Fermionic Quantum Computing
summary: Determining the highest amount of noise that quantum circuits can handle is an interesting and crucial task in the development of fault-tolerant quantum computation. Previous work has constrained this upper limit for local depolarizing noise to $\approx 45~\%$ for circuits constructed using the universal Clifford with T gate set by finding the noise threshold where the gate set loses universality. In this work, we use a similar method with the matchgate with non-Gaussian resource universal gate set to find a limit of $p=(8 - 2 \sqrt{6})/5$ or $\approx 62~\%$ for fermionic quantum computing that is independent of circuit depth. To do this, we use Uhlmann-Wootters concurrences for a 4-mode fermionic Choi state representing a resourceful gate combined with local depolarizing noise to determine when the combined channel is convex Gaussian. These bounds are not directly comparable due to differences in noise model making the bound of $\approx 62~\%$ the best known for fermions.

AI.tldr: This work derives an upper noise limit of p=(8−2√6)/5 ≈ 62% for fermionic quantum computing using a matchgate-plus-non-Gaussian-resource universal gate set, showing the bound is independent of circuit depth.
AI.motivation: Determining the maximum noise quantum circuits can tolerate is crucial for fault-tolerant quantum computation. Prior work bounded local depolarizing noise at ≈45% for Clifford+T circuits by locating where the gate set loses universality; an analogous bound was lacking for fermionic architectures.
AI.method: The authors adapt the universality-loss approach to the matchgate with non-Gaussian resource universal gate set. They compute Uhlmann-Wootters concurrences for a 4-mode fermionic Choi state representing a resourceful gate under local depolarizing noise, identifying when the combined channel becomes convex Gaussian.
AI.result: The analysis yields a noise limit of p=(8−2√6)/5 ≈ 62% for fermionic quantum computing, independent of circuit depth. Because of differing noise models, this bound is not directly comparable to the ≈45% result, but it is the best known bound for fermions.
AI.conclusion: The ≈62% threshold establishes the highest known tolerable noise for fermionic quantum computing, and the concurrence-based convex-Gaussianity criterion provides an effective tool for bounding noise limits in universal gate sets.

title: Certifying bipartite entanglement on a superconducting processor from a corrected QAOA cost layer
summary: The Quantum Approximate Optimisation Algorithm is the canonical near-term heuristic, yet on real superconducting hardware its behaviour is set by device physics, not by the algorithm. Hardware demonstrations rarely prove the intended coupling is realised, that genuine entanglement is prepared, or what controls it. We report a pre-registered single-device study on the nine-qubit superconducting processor Red at the Barcelona Supercomputing Center, using its five-qubit component. Across six calibrations we certify bipartite entanglement of a corrected QAOA cost layer on the good coupler at depth one by two-qubit tomographic negativity: 0.077, BCa 95% CI [0.065, 0.091], excluding zero every day, while the coupling-off twin stays separable and the degraded coupler equals zero. We then measure the device physics directly: in a pre-registered manipulation on a fixed Bell preparation (not the QAOA layer), reducing the CZ pulse amplitude causally reduces the certified negativity along a positive, well-fit slope (R^2 = 0.83-0.96), every rung-level interval excluding zero and surviving Holm and Benjamini-Hochberg correction. This is a local linearisation of a peaked response, not a global monotone law: the negativity peaks at conditional phase |zeta| = pi, which the nominal amplitude overshoots. The J=0 twin is a separate off-state control and the fringe visibility is constant, so the effect is coherent. The average gate fidelity is non-monotone in the drive and is reported only as a diagnostic. A per-circuit statevector guardrail excludes a diagonal compilation fault we disclose and repair. A randomized-measurement witness is consistent with entanglement but underpowered. The certificate collapses by depth three, and a pre-registered sixteen-instance depth-three ensemble shows no optimisation signal (one-sided Wilcoxon p = 0.15). We claim no advantage; the instances are classically trivial.

AI.tldr: A pre-registered single-device study on a five-qubit component of the nine-qubit superconducting processor Red certifies genuine bipartite entanglement in a corrected QAOA cost layer at depth one, and demonstrates causal control of that entanglement by CZ pulse amplitude, but finds the certificate collapses by depth three with no optimisation signal.
AI.motivation: Hardware demonstrations of QAOA rarely prove that the intended coupling is realised, that genuine entanglement is prepared, or what controls it, since device physics rather than the algorithm often governs behaviour on real superconducting hardware.
AI.method: Certify bipartite entanglement of a corrected QAOA cost layer across six calibrations via two-qubit tomographic negativity with BCa confidence intervals; use coupling-off twins and a degraded coupler as controls; run a pre-registered manipulation on a fixed Bell preparation varying CZ pulse amplitude; apply positive-slope fitting with Holm and Benjamini-Hochberg correction; use a per-circuit statevector guardrail, a randomized-measurement witness, and a pre-registered sixteen-instance depth-three ensemble with one-sided Wilcoxon testing.
AI.result: Certified negativity of 0.077 (BCa 95% CI [0.065, 0.091]) excluding zero every day, while the coupling-off twin remains separable and the degraded coupler equals zero; reducing CZ pulse amplitude causally reduces certified negativity along a positive well-fit slope (R^2 = 0.83-0.96), with all interval levels excluding zero and surviving multiple-comparison correction; the negativity peaks at conditional phase |zeta| = pi which nominal amplitude overshoots; the J=0 twin is a separate off-state control and fringe visibility is constant; average gate fidelity is non-monotone and diagnostic only; the randomized-measurement witness is consistent but underpowered; the certificate collapses by depth three and the depth-three ensemble shows no optimisation signal (one-sided Wilcoxon p = 0.15).
AI.conclusion: The study claims no advantage, as the instances are classically trivial, but provides certified entanglement and direct evidence of device-physics control over the QAOA cost layer at depth one, with entanglement certification degrading at greater depth.

title: Sub-extensive non-stabilizerness in the Dyck-Fredkin spin chain
summary: The stabilizer Rényi entropy is a quantitative measure of non-stabilizerness, or magic, and has typically been found to scale extensively with system size $N$ (i.e., $Θ(N)$) for a variety of many-body quantum states. In this note, we study the stabilizer Rényi entropy of the ground state of the spin-$\frac{1}{2}$ Dyck-Fredkin chain and its $t$-deformation, a local frustration-free model with unusual spectral-gap scaling. Exploiting the combinatorial structure, we carry out numerically exact finite-size calculations, which indicate asymptotic behavior depending on $t$: $Θ(N)$ for $t<1$, $Θ(\log N)$ at $t=1$, and $Θ(1)$ for $t>1$. The scaling at $t=1$ could be another manifestation of the unconventional criticality of the model, while the contrast with the behavior of the entanglement entropy suggests that non-stabilizerness might provide a new window into quantum many-body systems.

AI.tldr: The stabilizer Rényi entropy of the spin-1/2 Dyck-Fredkin chain ground state (and its t-deformation) shows t-dependent scaling: Θ(N) for t<1, Θ(log N) at t=1, and Θ(1) for t>1.
AI.motivation: Stabilizer Rényi entropy measures non-stabilizerness (magic) and typically scales extensively, Θ(N), with system size for many-body quantum states. The authors aim to characterize how this measure behaves in a local frustration-free model with unusual spectral-gap scaling, and to probe whether non-stabilizerness offers a distinct diagnostic beyond entanglement entropy.
AI.method: The authors study the ground state of the spin-1/2 Dyck-Fredkin chain and its t-deformation. Exploiting the model's combinatorial structure, they perform numerically exact finite-size calculations of the stabilizer Rényi entropy.
AI.result: The finite-size calculations indicate asymptotic scaling depending on t: Θ(N) for t<1, Θ(log N) at t=1, and Θ(1) for t>1.
AI.conclusion: The t=1 scaling may reflect the model's unconventional criticality, and the contrast with entanglement entropy behavior suggests non-stabilizerness can provide a new window into quantum many-body systems.

title: From Certifying Rank $k$ Projectors To Non-Positivity, Entanglement, And Non-Hermitian Witnesses Through Traces Of Matrix Powers
summary: We all know that a density matrix $ρ$ is pure if and only if $\mathrm{Tr} \,ρ^2 = 1$. But is this the only way to prove the purity of $ρ$ using the trace of its powers? Here I systematically study the necessary and sufficient conditions of the more general question of guaranteeing that all eigenvalues of a Hermitian matrix belong to a specified set through its trace of powers. More importantly, these characterization results are automatically witnesses certifying a quantum state as entangled, a Hermitian operator has least one negative eigenvalue and a linear operator as non-Hermitian. I demonstrate the effectiveness of these witnesses, analyze their performance, and study their strength, weakness together with resource requirement through numerical simulation as well as analytical work. I also discuss briefly the effects of numerical stability, uncertainty in measurement and rounding errors on these problems.

AI.tldr: The paper systematically characterizes necessary and sufficient conditions under which the traces of powers of a Hermitian matrix certify that all its eigenvalues lie in a specified set, and shows these results automatically yield entanglement witnesses, negative-eigenvalue certificates, and non-Hermiticity witnesses.
AI.motivation: The familiar purity criterion Tr(ρ²)=1 is only one instance of using trace-of-powers to control a density matrix's spectrum. There is no general theory of when such trace conditions are necessary and sufficient, and such a theory would also serve as a certificate for other properties (entanglement, negativity, non-Hermiticity).
AI.method: Systematically derive necessary and sufficient conditions guaranteeing that all eigenvalues of a Hermitian matrix belong to a specified set, expressed via traces of powers. Then reinterpret these characterizations as witnesses for entanglement, for a Hermitian operator having at least one negative eigenvalue, and for non-Hermiticity of a linear operator.
AI.result: The characterization results automatically act as the desired witnesses. Their effectiveness and performance are demonstrated and their strength, weakness and resource requirements are analyzed through numerical simulation and analytical work, with brief discussion of numerical stability, measurement uncertainty, and rounding errors.
AI.conclusion: Trace-of-powers conditions provide a unified, general framework for spectrum-set membership that doubles as a family of quantum and operator witnesses, whose practical merits and limitations are assessed both numerically and analytically.

title: Momentum-resolved quantum noise spectroscopy using ensembles of diamond quantum sensors
summary: Spatiotemporal fluctuations across multiple scales govern and characterize the emergent properties, phase boundaries, and low-energy excitations of strongly correlated matter. However, capturing these dynamics has remained a major experimental challenge, as conventional probes typically offer either high spatial or temporal resolution, but not both simultaneously. Here, we leverage high-fidelity wide-field imaging of dense diamond nitrogen vacancy center ensembles to measure the momentum and frequency power spectral density of magnetic fluctuations. To access spatial wavevectors below the diffraction limit, we tune the sensing volume continuously through optical depletion. This approach enables study of equilibrium and driven fluctuations across three orders of magnitude in spatial scale and tunable frequency bands, providing a direct means to map low-energy, long-wavelength fluctuations in correlated systems.

AI.tldr: Wide-field imaging of dense NV-center ensembles measures the momentum- and frequency-resolved power spectral density of magnetic fluctuations, using optical depletion to access sub-diffraction wavevectors across three orders of spatial magnitude.
AI.motivation: Spatiotemporal fluctuations across multiple scales govern emergent properties, phase boundaries, and low-energy excitations in strongly correlated matter, yet conventional probes offer either high spatial or high temporal resolution, not both simultaneously, leaving these dynamics experimentally hard to capture.
AI.method: High-fidelity wide-field imaging of dense diamond nitrogen-vacancy (NV) center ensembles to measure the momentum and frequency power spectral density of magnetic fluctuations. The sensing volume is tuned continuously via optical depletion to reach spatial wavevectors below the diffraction limit.
AI.result: Equilibrium and driven fluctuations are studied across three orders of magnitude in spatial scale and over tunable frequency bands.
AI.conclusion: The approach provides a direct means to map low-energy, long-wavelength fluctuations in correlated systems with simultaneous spatial and temporal resolution.

title: ECDSA.Fail: Open Autoresearch for Optimizing Elliptic-Curve Point Addition in Shor's Algorithm
comment: 62 pages, 10 figures. Project website and latest results: https://ecdsa.fail and source code: https://github.com/Layr-Labs/ecdsafail-challenge
summary: We propose Open Autoresearch, a paradigm in which humans and AI agents publish evaluator-verified improvements to a public leaderboard. We instantiate it in ECDSA.Fail, optimizing reversible secp256k1 point-addition circuits, a bottleneck in Shor's algorithm for elliptic-curve cryptography. The benchmark minimizes the spacetime-inspired score $S=Q\times T$, where $Q$ is peak logical qubit width and $T$ is average executed Toffoli count. Participants reduced $S$ by 86.1%. At the data cutoff (26 July 2026), the best-scoring circuit uses 1,151 qubits and 1,299,453 average executed Toffoli gates, giving $Q\times T\approx1.496$ billion. This is more than 50% below Google's published point-addition score thresholds (arXiv:2603.28846), under different accounting conventions. Because the benchmark supplies one addend classically, we construct a coherent windowed-addition-compatible variant implementing the single-call interface required by windowed Shor. It uses 1,162 qubits and 1,684,161 average executed Toffoli gates. On 100,000 random inputs, its empirical success probability is $\hat{p}=0.99809$, giving $Q\times T/\hat{p}\approx1.961$ billion under an independently rerunnable per-call sensitivity model, not a full-Shor success estimate. Its qubit and Toffoli counts lie below Google's published thresholds and Schrottenloher's reported operating points (arXiv:2606.02235), although differing interfaces, accounting conventions, and validation scope preclude formal dominance. After the cutoff, the score was further reduced to 1.259 billion, while a separate low-width circuit reached 813 qubits. The public record shows AI agents complementing human judgment, providing evidence for open autoresearch on efficiently evaluable, machine-checkable objectives.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "Open Autoresearch," a human-AI collaborative paradigm for publishing evaluator-verified leaderboard improvements, instantiated via the ECDSA.Fail benchmark optimizing reversible secp256k1 point-addition circuits for Shor's algorithm.
AI.motivation: Reversible secp256k1 point-addition circuits are a key bottleneck in Shor's algorithm for elliptic-curve cryptography. The authors aim to test whether an open, machine-checkable, leaderboard-driven research process (with AI agents complementing human judgment) can drive rapid, verifiable optimization on such objectives.
AI.method: They define a benchmark minimizing a spacetime-inspired score S = Q × T (Q = peak logical qubit width, T = average executed Toffoli count) and have humans and AI agents publish evaluator-verified improvements. They also construct a coherent windowed-addition-compatible variant meeting the single-call interface required by windowed Shor, and evaluate success probability over 100,000 random inputs under an independently rerunnable per-call sensitivity model.
AI.result: Participants reduced S by 86.1%. At cutoff (26 July 2026), the best circuit uses 1,151 qubits and 1,299,453 average executed Toffolis (Q×T ≈ 1.496 billion). The windowed-compatible variant uses 1,162 qubits and 1,684,161 average Toffolis, with empirical success probability p̂ = 0.99809, giving Q×T/p̂ ≈ 1.961 billion. Post-cutoff, S fell to 1.259 billion and a low-width circuit reached 813 qubits.
AI.conclusion: The results show AI agents complementing human judgment in an open, evaluator-verified setting, providing evidence for open autoresearch on efficiently evaluable, machine-checkable objectives. Comparisons with prior thresholds are suggestive but not formally dominant due to differing interfaces, accounting conventions, and validation scope.

title: Thermal Quantum Sensing: Fisher Information and Work Beyond Gaussian Signals
summary: Understanding how thermal fluctuations modify or suppress quantum-enhanced sensing is a central problem in quantum metrology. Closely related questions arise in quantum thermodynamics, particularly regarding the relation between the work induced by a signal and the information acquired by a sensor. Here, we establish general relations among the sensitivity of thermal quantum states, as quantified by different quantum Fisher information metrics, their temperature dependence, and the work induced by a unitary signal. We further show that, at high temperature, all monotone QFI metrics coincide to leading order with a universal quantity that can be expressed as the variance of a simple observable and itself defines a lesser-known QFI metric. This emergent uniqueness is reminiscent of the uniqueness of classical Fisher information in information geometry. In continuous-variable systems, the infinite-temperature limit is finite and generically non-zero for quadratic Gaussian signals, while it diverges for higher-degree signals. Remarkably, for any purely quadratic signal generator, the infinite-temperature QFI is at least twice the zero-temperature SLD QFI or, equivalently, at least eight times the ground-state variance of the generator. Consequently, the Cramér--Rao lower bound on the estimator variance is reduced by at least a factor of two. We illustrate these results using harmonic chains of bosonic modes relevant to trapped-ion platforms and quantum field-theoretic models.
