title: Information-geometric bounds on nonequilibrium relaxation in quantum Markov dynamics
summary: In this paper, we study the quantum information-geometric structure underlying short-time nonequilibrium relaxation in quantum Markov dynamics, and derive bounds on the nonequilibrium correction to the short-time relaxation curvature. These bounds generalize the information-geometric structure underlying Auconi's classical nonequilibrium relaxation inequality to quantum Markov dynamics. We consider the von Neumann relative entropy as quantum divergence, and parametrize perturbations through the Kubo-Mori map, which converts the second-order expansion of the relative entropy into the Bogoliubov-Kubo-Mori (BKM) inner product at all temperatures. For a quantum Markov semigroup with full-rank stationary state, the induced tangent-space generator admits a canonical decomposition into a BKM-symmetric and a BKM-antisymmetric part, and the leading nonequilibrium curvature correction takes the exact form of the expectation of the commutator between the dissipative and the transport part of the generator. This correction is bounded by the product of a BKM-symmetric dissipative activity and a transport-sector activity. The bound is verified on a noncommuting qubit model and a driven-dissipative qutrit, and the full chain is confirmed numerically on a two-dimensional Fokker-Planck steady state. In the high-temperature and overdamped limit the quantum formula reduces to the position-space Fokker-Planck expression and reproduces Auconi's entropy-production bound with the correct temperature factor.

AI.motivation: Auconi's classical nonequilibrium relaxation inequality has an information-geometric foundation, but no quantum generalization existed. The authors aim to extend this structure to quantum Markov dynamics and connect it to quantum divergence geometry.
AI.method: Using von Neumann relative entropy as the quantum divergence and the Kubo-Mori map for perturbations, the second-order expansion is converted into the Bogoliubov-Kubo-Mori (BKM) inner product at all temperatures. For a full-rank stationary quantum Markov semigroup, the tangent-space generator is decomposed into BKM-symmetric and antisymmetric parts, and the leading curvature correction is expressed as an expectation of the commutator between dissipative and transport generator parts.
AI.result: The nonequilibrium curvature correction is bounded by the product of a BKM-symmetric dissipative activity and a transport-sector activity. The bound is verified on a noncommuting qubit model and a driven-dissipative qutrit, and the full chain is confirmed numerically on a two-dimensional Fokker-Planck steady state.
AI.conclusion: In the high-temperature and overdamped limit, the quantum formula reduces to the position-space Fokker-Planck expression and recovers Auconi's entropy-production bound with the correct temperature factor, establishing a quantum information-geometric generalization of classical nonequilibrium relaxation inequalities.

title: Convex-Gaussianity of fermionic Gibbs states in perturbation theory
summary: We study the structure of Gibbs states in weakly perturbed interacting fermionic systems. First, for a sparse Hamiltonian $H=H_0+V$ with a quadratic term $H_0$ and a non-quadratic perturbation $V$ of scale $ε$, we show that the Gibbs state $ρ_β$ decomposes into a convex combination of Gaussian states whenever the inverse temperature satisfies $β\le O(\log(1/ε))$. Moreover, we prove that this bound is asymptotically tight by establishing that $β\le Θ(\log(1/ε))$ is necessary for certain sparse Hamiltonians. This general framework applies directly to the weak-coupling (small-$\vert{}U\vert{}$) regime of the Fermi--Hubbard model with hopping $t$ and on-site interaction $U$ on any graph of maximum degree $D$. Complementarily, in the strong-coupling (small-$\vert{}t\vert{}$) regime, we show that the Gibbs state remains convex-Gaussian up to $β\le O\big(\vert{}U\vert{}^{-1}\log(\vert{}U\vert{}/(D\vert{}t\vert{}))\big)$, revealing a mechanism for convex-Gaussianity distinct from the weak-coupling setting.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that Gibbs states of weakly perturbed interacting fermionic systems decompose into convex combinations of Gaussian states up to inverse temperature β ≤ O(log(1/ε)), with this bound shown to be asymptotically tight, and applies these results to both weak- and strong-coupling regimes of the Fermi–Hubbard model.
AI.motivation: Understanding whether Gibbs states of interacting fermionic systems can be represented as convex combinations of Gaussian (free-fermion) states is central to quantum many-body physics and simulation. Previous bounds were limited, and it was unclear how temperature and interaction strength constrain such convex-Gaussian decompositions across weak- and strong-coupling regimes.
AI.method: The authors consider a sparse Hamiltonian H = H0 + V with a quadratic part H0 and a non-quadratic perturbation V of scale ε. They analyze the structure of the Gibbs state ρβ via decomposition techniques to establish conditions on β under which ρβ is convex-Gaussian (a convex combination of Gaussian states). They also construct sparse Hamiltonians to prove asymptotic tightness, and apply the framework to the Fermi–Hubbard model with hopping t and on-site interaction U on graphs of maximum degree D in both weak- and strong-coupling limits.

In the strong-coupling (small |t|) regime, ρβ remains convex-Gaussian up to β ≤ O(|U|^{-1} log(|U|/(D|t|))), revealing a distinct mechanism for convex-Gaussianity.
AI.conclusion: Gibbs states of weakly perturbed interacting fermionic systems admit convex-Gaussian decompositions up to an inverse temperature that scales logarithmically with the perturbation strength, and this threshold is asymptotically optimal. The framework unifies weak- and strong-coupling behavior of the Fermi–Hubbard model, with the strong-coupling regime exhibiting a qualitatively different mechanism for convex-Gaussianity.

title: A Sum-of-Squares Hierarchy with Quadratic Convergence for Quantum Channel Coding
summary: Computing the optimal success probability for transmitting classical messages through a single use of a quantum channel is NP-hard, even for two messages. An existing semidefinite programming hierarchy based on symmetric extensions provides convergent upper bounds with an a priori error estimate that decays as the inverse square root of the extension level. In this work, we construct a Hermitian sum-of-squares hierarchy for an arbitrary number of messages and prove quadratic convergence in its level. The error bound is proportional to the advantage over random guessing. Our approach combines state-discrimination duality with positive polynomial kernels on products of spheres to construct feasible polynomial dual certificates. For binary messages, the resulting bounds give a multiplicative approximation from above of the trace-norm contraction coefficient.

AI.tldr: The paper constructs a Hermitian sum-of-squares hierarchy for computing optimal success probabilities in quantum channel discrimination with an arbitrary number of messages, achieving quadratic convergence in the hierarchy level and providing error bounds proportional to the advantage over random guessing.
AI.motivation: Computing the optimal success probability for transmitting classical messages through a single use of a quantum channel is NP-hard, even for two messages. The existing semidefinite programming hierarchy based on symmetric extensions only gives convergent upper bounds with an error estimate decaying as the inverse square root of the extension level, and applies mainly to two messages.
AI.method: They construct a Hermitian sum-of-squares hierarchy for an arbitrary number of messages. The approach combines state-discrimination duality with positive polynomial kernels on products of spheres to construct feasible polynomial dual certificates.
AI.result: The hierarchy achieves quadratic convergence in its level, improving over the inverse-square-root convergence of the symmetric-extension hierarchy. For binary messages, the resulting bounds give a multiplicative approximation from above of the trace-norm contraction coefficient.
AI.conclusion: The proposed Hermitian sum-of-squares hierarchy provides tighter, faster-converging upper bounds on optimal success probabilities, with error proportional to the advantage over random guessing, and extends to an arbitrary number of messages.

title: Perfect State Transfer from a Localised Two-Excitation State to a Dicke State via Static Spin-Network Hamiltonians
summary: I construct a family of time-independent, excitation-preserving spin Hamiltonians that realises perfect state transfer from a localised two-excitation state to the symmetric two-excitation Dicke state, for every system size $N \ge 4$. The Hamiltonian has the physical form $H = \sum_{i<j} J_{ij} (σ_i^+ σ_j^- + σ_j^+ σ_i^-) + \sum_i ε_i n_i$ with real couplings, and satisfies $e^{-iHt} |110\cdots0\rangle = e^{iφ} |D_N^{(2)}\rangle$ at a finite time. The construction exploits an $S_{N-2}$ permutation symmetry acting on the initially unoccupied spins, which reduces the dynamics to a four-dimensional invariant subspace. Requiring $(|ψ_0\rangle + |D_N^{(2)}\rangle)/2$ to be a zero eigenvector determines the on-site energies in closed form and leaves three coupling parameters free. The remaining inverse spectral problem reduces to two polynomial equations in two dimensionless coupling ratios; eliminating one ratio yields a degree-six reciprocal polynomial, which the substitution $z = x + x^{-1}$ converts to a cubic. For the spectral family $(-n,-1,1)$, with $n$ an odd integer, an explicit factorisation of the leading coefficient together with a boundary evaluation at $z=-2$ shows that for every $N \ge 4$ an odd $n$ can be chosen large enough that a real root with $z < -2$ exists; a subresultant argument supplies a real lift of that root to the original system. The existence proof is entirely symbolic and does not rely on numerical optimisation; direct propagation is used only as independent validation. The result is a constrained analogue of perfect state transfer: unlike the general real-state problem, where an unconstrained real symmetric matrix suffices, here the Hamiltonian is required to arise from an excitation-preserving spin-network form.

AI.tldr: A family of time-independent, excitation-preserving spin Hamiltonians achieves perfect state transfer from a localised two-excitation state to the symmetric Dicke state for all N ≥ 4, proven symbolically.
AI.motivation: Perfect state transfer is typically studied with unconstrained real symmetric matrices, but the question is whether it remains achievable when the Hamiltonian must arise from a physically constrained excitation-preserving spin-network form. The paper asks whether an explicit, symbolic construction exists for transferring a two-excitation state to the Dicke state at every system size.

Imposing that (|ψ0⟩ + |D_N^(2)⟩)/2 is a zero eigenvector fixes on-site energies in closed form, leaving three free coupling parameters. For the family (-n,-1,1) with odd integer n, an explicit factorisation and a boundary evaluation at z = -2 show a real root with z < -2 exists, and a subresultant argument gives a real lift.

Direct propagation validates the symbolic proof independently, confirming perfect state transfer e^{-iHt}|110...0⟩ = e^{iφ}|D_N^(2)⟩ at a finite time.
AI.conclusion: Perfect state transfer to the two-excitation Dicke state is achievable under the constrained excitation-preserving spin-network form for all N ≥ 4. This constitutes a constrained analogue of the general real-state problem, with an entirely symbolic existence proof requiring no numerical optimisation.

title: Realization Theory for Quantum Filtering: Classifying Continuously Monitored Bosonic Systems
summary: Exact finite-dimensional descriptions exist for a few important classes of continuously monitored quantum systems, but there is no general criterion separating systems that admit such filters from those that do not. We formulate this question as a realization problem and introduce the linearized observable Hankel operator $K_O$, which maps changes in the past measurement record to changes in a future conditional observable. For polynomial bosonic systems under continuous quadrature monitoring, this gives a sharp boundary between finite and infinite realizability. Gaussian dynamics and the Conditional Momentum Moment class admit exact finite-dimensional filters, while nonlinear dynamics outside these classes generically produce infinitely many independent response directions and admit no robust finite-dimensional $C^1$ observable- or state-level filter. The singular values of $K_O$ then extend the same realization framework to approximation, giving the optimal rank-$d$ local-response error beyond the finite classes. Numerical experiments with the Kerr and Duffing oscillators, together with a dynamics-adapted Poisson--Charlier construction for Kerr dynamics, show how this observable-level benchmark interacts with concrete reduced representations. Together, these results identify the boundary of exact quantum filtering and quantify finite-dimensional approximation beyond it.

AI.motivation: Exact finite-dimensional descriptions exist only for a few classes of continuously monitored quantum systems, and no general criterion distinguishes systems admitting such filters from those that do not; the paper seeks to fill this gap by providing a principled boundary between finite and infinite realizability.
AI.method: The filtering question is cast as a realization problem, introducing the linearized observable Hankel operator K_O that maps changes in the past measurement record to changes in a future conditional observable. Singular values of K_O extend the realization framework to approximation, yielding optimal rank-d local-response error.

title: Cascade-induced high-performance nonreciprocal quantum batteries
summary: Nonreciprocal quantum batteries harness reservoir engineering for controlled energy transfer, heralding a paradigm shift for quantum energy storage. A prior study utilizing the Metelmann-Clerk formalism reported a fourfold enhancement in nonreciprocal energy accumulation over reciprocal counterparts. This fourfold enhancement, however, appears to stem from a Lindblad master equation that exhibits fundamental inconsistencies, which may systematically understate the actual nonreciprocal advantage. Our approach is rooted in the rigorously established cascaded open quantum systems formalism, which ensures both mathematical consistency and physical fidelity. Remarkably, we surpass the previously reported fourfold benchmark, attaining a regime-independent sixteenfold steady-state nonreciprocal energy advantage over reciprocal systems. We further uncover a dissipation-dependent battery-to-charger efficiency, fourfold under symmetric damping, surpassing this benchmark when the battery is less dissipative, and lower otherwise. This work establishes the cascaded formalism as a mathematically rigorous and experimentally viable foundation for high-performance quantum energy storage.

AI.tldr: This paper reformulates nonreciprocal quantum batteries using the cascaded open quantum systems formalism, showing the prior fourfold enhancement benchmark was based on an inconsistent Lindblad master equation and instead achieving a sixteenfold steady-state nonreciprocal energy advantage.
AI.motivation: A previous study using the Metelmann-Clerk formalism claimed a fourfold enhancement in nonreciprocal energy accumulation, but its Lindblad master equation contains fundamental inconsistencies that may systematically understate the true nonreciprocal advantage. A mathematically consistent and physically faithful framework is therefore needed.
AI.method: The authors adopt the rigorously established cascaded open quantum systems formalism, which guarantees mathematical consistency and physical fidelity, to analyze steady-state nonreciprocal energy accumulation and battery-to-charger efficiency.
AI.result: The proposed approach surpasses the prior fourfold benchmark, reaching a regime-independent sixteenfold steady-state nonreciprocal energy advantage over reciprocal systems. It also reveals a dissipation-dependent battery-to-charger efficiency: fourfold under symmetric damping, exceeding this benchmark when the battery is less dissipative, and lower otherwise.
AI.conclusion: The cascaded formalism provides a mathematically rigorous and experimentally viable foundation for high-performance quantum energy storage, correcting the inconsistencies of the earlier Lindblad treatment and establishing a stronger nonreciprocal advantage.

title: Enhancing Pauli Correlation Encoding for quantum optimization via systematic expressivity analysis
summary: Quantum approaches for combinatorial optimization problems have attracted considerable attention in recent years. Among these approaches, Pauli Correlation Encoding (PCE) has emerged as a promising framework for quantum devices with limited qubit resources because it embeds optimization variables in expectation values of Pauli strings. However, the mechanisms underlying its performance and the reasons for its saturation remain unclear. In this work, we investigate these questions through a systematic analysis of expressivity and trainability. First, we compare PCE with classical surrogate models based on tensor networks whose structures progressively approach the topology of the PCE circuit. The results show that PCE attains comparable solution quality with substantially fewer trainable parameters, indicating strong parameter efficiency. Second, to determine whether the performance saturation of conventional PCE is caused by insufficient expressivity or by optimization difficulty, we perform a diagnostic expressivity test in which the circuit is trained toward reference configurations for Max-Cut. The results show that even shallow PCE circuits can represent strong solutions, indicating that the main bottleneck is not the representational power of the ansatz, but the trainability under the relaxed objective function. Motivated by this finding, we propose a multistage continuation framework that gradually transforms a smooth relaxed objective into a sharper objective that more closely approximates the target discrete problem. Numerical experiments on G-set instances with 800 vertices show that the proposed method consistently outperforms conventional PCE and is competitive with representative graph neural network (GNN) methods. These results clarify the main factors behind PCE performance and provide a practical strategy for improving PCE on quantum devices with limited qubit resources.

AI.tldr: This work analyzes Pauli Correlation Encoding (PCE) for combinatorial optimization, showing its bottleneck is trainability rather than expressivity, and proposes a multistage continuation framework that outperforms conventional PCE on 800-vertex G-set instances.
AI.motivation: PCE is promising for quantum devices with limited qubit resources since it embeds optimization variables in expectation values of Pauli strings, but the mechanisms behind its performance and the causes of its saturation remain unclear.
AI.method: A systematic analysis of expressivity and trainability was conducted. PCE was compared with classical tensor-network surrogate models whose structures progressively approach the PCE circuit topology. A diagnostic expressivity test trained the circuit toward Max-Cut reference configurations. Based on the finding that trainability is the bottleneck, a multistage continuation framework was proposed that gradually transforms a smooth relaxed objective into a sharper objective approximating the target discrete problem.
AI.result: PCE achieved comparable solution quality with substantially fewer trainable parameters than tensor-network surrogates, indicating strong parameter efficiency. Shallow PCE circuits could represent strong solutions, showing the main bottleneck is trainability under the relaxed objective rather than representational power. On G-set instances with 800 vertices, the proposed method consistently outperformed conventional PCE and was competitive with representative GNN methods.
AI.conclusion: The main factors behind PCE performance are clarified, with trainability identified as the key bottleneck, and a practical multistage continuation strategy is provided for improving PCE on quantum devices with limited qubit resources.

title: Generalized Fidelity and the Data Processing Inequality
summary: In this note, we show that the generalized Bures--Wasserstein distance induced by the generalized fidelity does not satisfy the data processing inequality in dimensions greater than two. In dimension two, although we do not settle the DPI in full generality, we derive two sufficient conditions guaranteeing it by using an explicit formula for the real part of the generalized fidelity. Furthermore, we find a necessary and sufficient condition under which the generalized fidelity reduces to the Uhlmann fidelity.

AI.tldr: The generalized Bures–Wasserstein distance induced by the generalized fidelity violates the data processing inequality in dimensions greater than two; in dimension two, two sufficient conditions for the DPI are derived, along with a necessary and sufficient condition for the generalized fidelity to reduce to the Uhlmann fidelity.
AI.motivation: The generalized Bures–Wasserstein distance and the generalized fidelity are natural extensions of their standard counterparts, and whether they obey the data processing inequality (DPI) is a fundamental question for their use as distinguishability or resource measures. This note aims to determine the validity of the DPI for this generalized distance.
AI.method: A counterexample is constructed to show failure of the DPI for the generalized Bures–Wasserstein distance in dimensions greater than two. For dimension two, an explicit formula for the real part of the generalized fidelity is derived and used to establish two sufficient conditions for the DPI. A necessary and sufficient condition for the generalized fidelity to coincide with the Uhlmann fidelity is also characterized.
AI.result: The generalized Bures–Wasserstein distance does not satisfy the data processing inequality for dimensions greater than two. In dimension two, two sufficient conditions guaranteeing the DPI are obtained. A necessary and sufficient condition under which the generalized fidelity reduces to the Uhlmann fidelity is identified.
AI.conclusion: The DPI fails for the generalized Bures–Wasserstein distance beyond dimension two, so it cannot generally serve as a monotone under quantum channels. In the two-dimensional case the DPI holds under the derived sufficient conditions, and the generalized fidelity coincides with the Uhlmann fidelity exactly when the stated necessary and sufficient condition holds.

title: Split-Step Dirac Cellular Automata for Continuous-Time Dirac Dynamics on Finite Spatial Lattices
summary: Dirac Cellular Automata (DCA) provide a framework for simulating Dirac dynamics, yet the rigid coupling between spatial and temporal resolutions can introduce artificial phase-matching symmetries on finite grids that suppress interference phenomena such as Zitterbewegung. In this work, we propose a Split-Step Dirac Cellular Automaton (SDCA) that enables continuous-time Dirac evolution at fixed spatial discretization. By employing a Trotterized fractional-step scheme in the momentum representation, SDCA breaks the phase-matching cancellation present in the standard DCA and recovers the interference dynamics of the continuous-time limit. We benchmark the SDCA through analytical and numerical studies and demonstrate its implementation on IBM Quantum processors. Despite the increased circuit depth required for finer temporal resolution, the NISQ implementation reproduces the characteristic velocity oscillations and entanglement-entropy dynamics of the continuous-time model. We further investigate hardware-topology trade-offs and dynamic circuit implementations of the Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT), highlighting the competing effects of gate errors, measurement, and feed-forward latency. These results demonstrate that SDCA provides a practical framework for improving temporal resolution while maintaining a fixed spatial quantum register, enabling the exploration of relativistic quantum dynamics on near-term quantum devices.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a Split-Step Dirac Cellular Automaton (SDCA) that achieves continuous-time Dirac evolution at fixed spatial discretization, overcoming artificial phase-matching suppression of Zitterbewegung in standard DCA, and demonstrates it on IBM Quantum hardware.
AI.motivation: Standard Dirac Cellular Automata couple spatial and temporal resolutions rigidly. On finite grids this coupling induces artificial phase-matching symmetries that cancel interference phenomena such as Zitterbewegung, preventing faithful simulation of continuous-time Dirac dynamics.
AI.method: The authors propose SDCA, using a Trotterized fractional-step scheme in the momentum representation with a Split-Step Quantum Walk structure. This decouples temporal resolution from fixed spatial discretization, breaking the phase-matching cancellation. They benchmark analytically and numerically, then implement on IBM Quantum processors, studying hardware-topology trade-offs and dynamic-circuit QFT implementations.
AI.result: SDCA recovers the interference dynamics of the continuous-time limit. The NISQ implementation reproduces characteristic velocity oscillations (Zitterbewegung) and entanglement-entropy dynamics of the continuous-time model, despite increased circuit depth. Trade-offs among gate errors, measurement, and feed-forward latency are characterized.
AI.conclusion: SDCA offers a practical framework for improving temporal resolution while keeping a fixed spatial quantum register, enabling exploration of relativistic quantum dynamics on near-term quantum devices.

title: Small-Bias Quantum Approximate Counting via the Multiplicative Adversary Method
summary: We study the two-weight decision version of quantum approximate counting: given oracle access to $x\in\{0,1\}^N$, distinguish $|x|=M$ from $|x|=M+Δ$ with success probability $1/2+ζ$. Using the multiplicative adversary method, we prove $Ω\left(\max\left\{ζ\sqrt{(N-M)(M+Δ)}/Δ,\sqrt{ζN/Δ}\right\}\right)$. The same parameter dependence follows from the polynomial-method characterization of the two-layer symmetric function by Podder, Yao, and Ye. Our contribution is a multiplicative-adversary derivation that tracks the progress produced by individual oracle queries. For the first term, after complementing the input if necessary, we assume $M+Δ\le N-M$. We use the Hamming-layer subspaces from the eigenspace method of Ambainis, Spalek, and de Wolf and compose their adjacent-layer unitary maps to relate the two nonadjacent promise layers. After fixing the queried coordinate, the analysis block-diagonalizes into four-dimensional subspaces. An exact calculation of the one-query progress ratio gives the first lower bound. The same estimate also implies $\left\|(I-\widehatΠ_{\mathrm{bad}})\lvertΨ^T\rangle\right\|^2=O\left(T^2Δ^2/((N-M)(M+Δ))\right)$ for the coherent input superposition used in the adversary argument. For the second term, we prove directly using a three-eigenvalue multiplicative adversary that unique OR on $n$ bits with success probability $1/2+ζ$ requires $Ω(\sqrt{ζn})$ queries, and then reduce unique OR to the two-weight counting problem.

AI.tldr: The paper proves a two-weight lower bound for quantum approximate counting via a multiplicative adversary method that tracks per-query progress, recovering the known parameter dependence.
AI.motivation: The two-weight decision version of quantum approximate counting already had a lower bound derivable from the polynomial-method characterization of the two-layer symmetric function by Podder, Yao, and Ye. The authors seek a direct multiplicative-adversary derivation that tracks the progress produced by individual oracle queries, providing an alternative and more granular proof of the same parameter dependence.
AI.method: Using the multiplicative adversary method, the authors analyze the two-weight decision problem: given oracle access to x∈{0,1}^N, distinguish |x|=M from |x|=M+Δ with success probability 1/2+ζ. For the first term, after complementing the input if necessary so that M+Δ≤N−M, they use Hamming-layer subspaces from the eigenspace method of Ambainis, Spalek, and de Wolf and compose adjacent-layer unitary maps to relate the two nonadjacent promise layers. Fixing the queried coordinate yields a block-diagonalization into four-dimensional subspaces, and an exact one-query progress ratio gives the first lower bound. This estimate also bounds the projection of the coherent input superposition onto the bad subspace. For the second term, they use a three-eigenvalue multiplicative adversary to show unique OR on n bits requires Ω(√(ζn)) queries, then reduce unique OR to the two-weight counting problem.

AI.conclusion: The authors provide a multiplicative-adversary derivation of the two-weight approximate counting lower bound, matching the parameter dependence obtained via the polynomial-method characterization. The proof tracks individual oracle-query progress through Hamming-layer subspace composition and a block-diagonal four-dimensional analysis.

title: Electrically tunable, two-photon interference from remote silicon-vacancy centers in industrial silicon carbide
comment: Main part: 19 pages, 4 figure groups; Supplementary Information: 23 pages, 9 figure groups
summary: Distributed quantum networks rely on spatially separated, independently operated quantum systems as network nodes, whose emitted photons must be interfered with high visibility to establish end-to-end entanglement. Crucially, for network-relevant applications, high visibilities must be achieved over prolonged timescales to reduce overheads for error correction, and to increase network rates. Here, we demonstrate experimentally that silicon vacancy $\mathrm{V_{Si}}$ color centers in silicon carbide (SiC) achieve these requirements, notably in a mass-deployable fashion. We integrate $\mathrm{V_{Si}}$ centers in different industrial-grade SiC p-i-n diodes, which are controlled via voltage biassing. This way, we demonstrate both, spectral overlapping of 19 randomly selected $\mathrm{V_{Si}}$ centers in different diodes, as well as spectral narrowing close to the lifetime limit, i.e., typically below 60 MHz. Notably, these performance parameters are long-term stable, e.g., readjusting the p-i-n diode bias is required only every 8.4 hours, which reduces significantly the overall experimental overhead. We then use these assets to demonstrate high-quality two-photon interference between $\mathrm{V_{Si}}$ centers located in two different cryostat setups, which are spatially separated by two meters. Notably, we perform a 26-days long measurement campaign, demonstrating two-photon interference with state-of-the-art raw interference visibilities of 82%, which aligns with the current state-of-the-art. These results establish $\mathrm{V_{Si}}$ centers in industry-grade SiC devices as a scalable, spectrally stable building block for distributed quantum networks.

AI.tldr: Silicon vacancy color centers in industrial-grade SiC p-i-n diodes achieve spectrally stable, high-visibility two-photon interference, establishing them as a scalable building block for distributed quantum networks.
AI.motivation: Distributed quantum networks require spatially separated, independently operated quantum nodes whose emitted photons interfere with high visibility. For network-relevant applications, this high visibility must be sustained over prolonged timescales to reduce error-correction overheads and boost network rates, a requirement not yet met in a mass-deployable fashion.
AI.method: The authors integrate silicon vacancy (V_Si) color centers into different industrial-grade SiC p-i-n diodes controlled by voltage biasing. They demonstrate spectral overlapping of 19 randomly selected V_Si centers across different diodes and spectral narrowing close to the lifetime limit (typically below 60 MHz). title: Dynamic Observable Subspaces: Fast Simulation of Observable Quantum Dynamics
summary: By decomposing quantum dynamics across the Lie orbits of a list of observables, we find polynomial bounded classical simulations for the dynamics of the quantum system given a polynomial sized dynamic Lie algebra (DLA) for the generators of the quantum system. To do so, we describe how to construct the Dynamic Observable Subspace (DOS) that captures all the relevant dynamics for calculating expectation values for a specific observable for Pauli strings, diffusor mixers, and general local generators. Efficient sparse matrix representation, decoupling nonlinearity from such representation and basis construction with permissible pruning allows us to simulate the closed dynamics of such systems with hundreds of qubits. Moreover, we find that while restricted DOS circuits may not express the space of an associated Hamiltonian, they can dramatically outperform a fully expressive circuit due to the absence of the Barren Plateau. While classically simulatable, such circuits can still exhibit a form of quantum advantage through inference, act as warm starting for more expressive circuits, and find high quality trial states for Quantum Amplitude Amplification or Quantum Phase Estimation. In the simulation of quantum dynamics, we find that our restricted circuit can be simulated in polynomial time while producing high quality guiding state for downstream tasks like Quantum Phase Estimation with significantly lower energy than circuits with full expressivity.

The authors aim to identify such structure—specifically polynomial-sized Dynamic Lie Algebras—and exploit it to simulate large quantum systems while retaining practical utility for downstream quantum tasks.
AI.method: They decompose quantum dynamics across the Lie orbits of a list of observables and construct a Dynamic Observable Subspace (DOS) that captures all dynamics relevant to computing expectation values. This construction is applied to Pauli strings, diffusor mixers, and general local generators. They use efficient sparse matrix representations, decouple nonlinearity from the representation, and build bases with permissible pruning.

They also produce high-quality guiding states for Quantum Phase Estimation with significantly lower energy.
AI.conclusion: Restricted DOS circuits are classically simulatable in polynomial time yet can exhibit a form of quantum advantage through inference, serve as warm starts for more expressive circuits, and provide high-quality trial states for Quantum Amplitude Amplification or Quantum Phase Estimation, outperforming fully expressive circuits in energy quality.

title: Robust Device-Independent Certification of Boolean-Phase Gates
summary: Device-independent certification of a quantum gate requires the input and output tests to identify the same reference qubits. Self-testing the output Choi state alone does not guarantee this consistency. Boolean derivatives convert the target-dependent phase information into classical signs that can be evaluated from local measurement outcomes. At maximal violation, the tests self-test the normalized Choi state and the measured observables. Away from the maximum, they give an explicit affine lower bound on the extracted-state squared fidelity that is uniform over all Boolean functions and valid in arbitrary local dimensions. We then combine an identity test and a gate-output test in an independent-source network in which the reference devices use the same physical observables, obtaining a closed-form Choi-fidelity bound for an effective \(n\)-qubit channel. For CCZ, a joint six-party analysis gives a stronger robustness bound without changing the Bell expression or measurement settings. The construction shows how the algebraic structure of a gate can shift target-dependent information from quantum measurement design to classical processing of local outcomes.

Existing approaches are therefore insufficient to certify a gate as a complete process.
AI.method: The authors target Boolean-phase gates, a broad family of computational-basis diagonal gates specified by Boolean functions. Boolean derivatives convert target-dependent phase information into classical signs evaluable from local measurement outcomes, yielding Bell tests built from CHSH blocks with two binary measurements per party and no entangling measurements. title: Minimax games for quantum channel discrimination
comment: This work integrates arXiv:2510.07977 and arXiv:2601.10243 in a unified framework and strengthens the results further
summary: Quantum channel discrimination is a primitive task for identifying, verifying, and benchmarking quantum dynamics. Previous studies have primarily considered either the best-case tester-input setting or the worst-case jammer-input setting. Here, we introduce a game-theoretic framework in which both the tester and jammer control separate inputs. Combining three input structures, characterized by whether the tester and jammer use entangled inputs or IID inputs across channel uses, with four information patterns, determined by the visibility of the jammer's strategy and its knowledge of the true hypothesis, yields twelve game models. We provide exact finite blocklength hypothesis testing characterizations of all twelve models in terms of nine minimax hypothesis testing divergences and derive their asymptotic Stein exponents. Notably, for entangled jammers, neither the visibility of the jammer's strategy nor its knowledge of the true hypothesis affects the asymptotic Stein exponent, whereas the information pattern remains consequential for IID jammers. As an example, we study the discrimination of a general channel from a replacer channel and show that all asymptotic Stein exponents coincide with the same additive, single letter quantity. We further develop a general argument that upgrades achievability results to strong converse results, thereby establishing strong converse properties for several game models, resolving an open problem in composite hypothesis testing posed by Berta et al. [Commun. Math. Phys. 385, 55 (2021)], and strengthening several recent results of Lami [arXiv:2510.06340]. The framework and techniques developed here may support future studies of quantum information tasks involving competing roles.

It provides exact finite blocklength hypothesis testing characterizations via nine minimax divergences, derives asymptotic Stein exponents, and develops a technique to upgrade achievability to strong converse.
AI.motivation: Prior work on quantum channel discrimination considered either a best-case tester-input setting or a worst-case jammer-input setting separately, lacking a unified framework where both parties actively control inputs. A framework capturing competing tester/jammer roles was needed to characterize discrimination performance under adversarial conditions and to resolve open questions in composite hypothesis testing.

For entangled jammers, neither jammer strategy visibility nor knowledge of the true hypothesis affects the asymptotic Stein exponent, whereas the information pattern remains consequential for IID jammers. For discrimination of a general channel from a replacer channel, all asymptotic Stein exponents coincide with the same additive, single-letter quantity.
AI.conclusion: The framework unifies best-case and worst-case channel discrimination and reveals how input structures and information patterns affect Stein exponents. The strong converse argument resolves an open problem in composite hypothesis testing posed by Berta et al. [Commun. Math. Phys. 385, 55 (2021)] and strengthens several recent results of Lami [arXiv:2510.06340]. title: Simple QKD keyrate computations from tangent-line bounds
summary: Recent work in quantum key distribution (QKD) has yielded finite-size keyrates based on convex optimisation problems, using the framework of entropy accumulation. Multiple solvers have been developed to address these optimisations in recent years, but have been based on a somewhat elaborate framework using sophisticated algorithms, in order to accommodate a broad range of QKD protocols. In this work, we note that for basic QKD protocols such as qubit BB84, the keyrates can be easily computed using off-the-shelf solvers instead, by obtaining suitable tangent lines to lower bound terms in the objective function. We compute the resulting finite-size keyrates and compare them to previous work. Moreover, we extend this approach to the six-state protocol, by deriving closed-form expressions for the single-round Rényi entropies in the protocol. This should facilitate subsequent study of the six-state protocol via entropy accumulation.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that for basic QKD protocols like qubit BB84, finite-size keyrates can be computed using off-the-shelf solvers by finding tangent lines to lower-bound objective terms, and extends this to the six-state protocol via closed-form single-round Rényi entropy expressions.
AI.motivation: Existing finite-size keyrate computations for QKD based on convex optimisation and entropy accumulation rely on elaborate, sophisticated frameworks and custom solvers designed for broad protocol coverage. This complexity is unnecessary for basic protocols, motivating a simpler approach.
AI.method: The authors obtain suitable tangent lines to lower bound terms in the objective function, enabling the use of off-the-shelf solvers for basic protocols such as qubit BB84. They extend this method to the six-state protocol by deriving closed-form expressions for the single-round Rényi entropies.
AI.result: The resulting finite-size keyrates are computed and compared against previous work. Closed-form single-round Rényi entropy expressions are derived for the six-state protocol.
AI.conclusion: Simpler, off-the-shelf solvers suffice for computing finite-size keyrates in basic QKD protocols via tangent-line lower bounds, and the approach extends to the six-state protocol, facilitating future study of it via entropy accumulation.

title: When Does a Quantum Speedup Survive End-to-End?
summary:
Primitive quantum speedups are interface-relative: they depend on the input access used to run the primitive and on the output contract used to consume its state or samples. This paper introduces a transcript-level admissibility relation \(A_M\preceq_{\mathrm{int}}A_Q\), defined relative to the declared implementation package of the quantum interface. It identifies which adaptive classical access transcripts that same package licenses, with all setup, transcript-generation, and precision overheads charged.
  The main application is an operational audit for normalized-Betti estimation in clique-complex TDA, separating three declared-interface regimes. Reversible indexed simplex interfaces certify matched classical simplex sampling and local Laplacian row access by evaluating their reversible routines on single computational branches. Membership-based preparations induce a rejection route of overhead \(\binom{n}{k+1}/|S_k|\). Abstract spectral or block-encoding interfaces require an accompanying implementation package, transcript reduction, or shared representation. Under the indexed certificate and interface closure, the end-to-end cost is fixed by the imported estimator's spectral dependence on the gap \(γ\); the concretely realized bounded-treewidth family already admits exact \(\mathrm{poly}(n)\) classical Betti computation by rank over \(\mathbb{Q}\). A low-rank separation supports the role of access and output contracts.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes "interface-relative" quantum speedups via a transcript-level admissibility relation \(A_M \preceq_{\mathrm{int}} A_Q\) tied to an interface's implementation package, and applies it as an operational audit for normalized-Betti estimation in clique-complex TDA across three declared-interface regimes.
AI.motivation: Primitive quantum speedups are not absolute: they depend on the input access used to run the primitive and the output contract used to consume its state or samples. The work aims to make this interface relativity precise and operationally auditable, particularly for TDA Betti estimation where claimed quantum advantages may hinge on undeclared access/output assumptions.
AI.method: Introduces a transcript-level admissibility relation \(A_M\preceq_{\mathrm{int}}A_Q\), defined relative to the declared implementation package of the quantum interface. It determines which adaptive classical access transcripts that package licenses, charging all setup, transcript-generation, and precision overheads. This is applied as an operational audit separating three declared-interface regimes for normalized-Betti estimation in clique-complex TDA.
AI.result: Reversible indexed simplex interfaces certify matched classical simplex sampling and local Laplacian row access by evaluating reversible routines on single computational branches. Membership-based preparations induce a rejection route with overhead \(\binom{n}{k+1}/|S_k|\). Abstract spectral or block-encoding interfaces require an accompanying implementation package, transcript reduction, or shared representation. Under the indexed certificate and interface closure, end-to-end cost is fixed by the imported estimator's spectral dependence on the gap \(\gamma\); the concretely realized bounded-treewidth family already admits exact \(\mathrm{poly}(n)\) classical Betti computation by rank over \(\mathbb{Q}\). A low-rank separation supports the role of access and output contracts.
AI.conclusion: Quantum speedups for Betti estimation are interface-relative and must be assessed against declared access and output contracts. Only when the interface is certified (e.g., reversible indexed simplex access under closure) does the end-to-end cost reduce to the imported estimator's spectral gap dependence, and in that regime concrete instances are classically tractable; uncertified abstract interfaces require additional implementation, transcript reduction, or shared representation.

title: From Block-encoding to Generalized Quantum Signal Processing: Principles, Algorithms and Applications
summary:
Modern quantum algorithms are increasingly formulated as coherent procedures for implementing polynomial transformations of operators and singular values. This perspective provides a powerful and unifying language for quantum algorithm design, connecting a wide range of distinct problems through five closely related key tools: block-encoding, qubitization, QSP, QSVT and GQSP. Block-encoding embeds non-unitary matrices into larger unitaries; qubitization converts block-encodings into structured operators; QSP, QSVT and GQSP enable polynomial transformations with near-optimal query complexity. Together, these techniques form a general toolkit for transforming matrix functions into implementable quantum circuits. This paper develops these techniques from first principles as a unified framework for constructing quantum algorithms. We apply this framework to representative applications to highlight design principles and demonstrate how distinct algorithms can be constructed from a unified sequence of operator transformations.
  A central contribution is a systematic decision workflow for selecting the appropriate approach according to the operator structure and the desired transformation polynomial. This perspective clarifies when direct GQSP or through qubitization, or Laurent expansion, or QSVT is most appropriate. We organize algorithmic design into an end-to-end pipeline: identifying the target matrix function, constructing an appropriate block-encoding, determining the relevant spectral domain, designing a polynomial or Laurent-polynomial approximation, synthesizing the phase factors, and translating the transformation into an executable quantum circuit. By applying this unified framework to example applications, we showcase a practical methodology for reasoning, designing, and implementing quantum algorithms based on polynomial transformations.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a unified framework for quantum algorithm design based on polynomial operator transformations, integrating block-encoding, qubitization, QSP, QSVT, and GQSP into an end-to-end design pipeline with a systematic decision workflow.
AI.motivation: Modern quantum algorithms are increasingly expressed as coherent procedures for polynomial transformations of operators and singular values, but the five key tools (block-encoding, qubitization, QSP, QSVT, GQSP) are often treated separately. A unified treatment is needed to connect distinct problems and clarify when each technique is most appropriate.
AI.method: The authors develop these techniques from first principles as a unified framework. They establish a systematic decision workflow for selecting the appropriate approach based on operator structure and desired transformation polynomial, and organize algorithmic design into an end-to-end pipeline: identifying the target matrix function, constructing a block-encoding, determining the spectral domain, designing a polynomial or Laurent-polynomial approximation, synthesizing phase factors, and translating the transformation into an executable quantum circuit.
AI.result: Block-encoding embeds non-unitary matrices into larger unitaries; qubitization converts block-encodings into structured operators; QSP, QSVT, and GQSP enable polynomial transformations with near-optimal query complexity. The framework clarifies when direct GQSP, qubitization, Laurent expansion, or QSVT is most appropriate, and demonstrates construction of distinct algorithms from a unified sequence of operator transformations.
AI.conclusion: The unified framework serves as a general toolkit transforming matrix functions into implementable quantum circuits, offering a practical methodology for reasoning, designing, and implementing quantum algorithms based on polynomial transformations, as illustrated through representative applications.

title: Fidelity-Aware Scheduling of Quantum Circuits on Multi-QPU Systems
comment: Accepted at the 2nd International Workshop for Software Frameworks and Workload Management on Quantum and HPC Ecosystems (SFWM), co-located with SC26
summary: High Performance Computing-Quantum Computing (HPCQC) platforms expose multiple Quantum Processing Units (QPUs) that may differ in size, topology, native gates, and noise characteristics. For current noisy devices, errors compound along the compiled circuits quickly, and minimizing them, that is, maximizing the circuits' execution fidelity, is essential for reliable results. Fidelity depends on the compilation to a specific target device: the same high-level circuit may produce different executables and, therefore, different expected fidelities across QPUs. We present a low-overhead fidelity-aware scheduling framework for multi-QPU systems based on a Graph Neural Network (GNN) that estimates, before compilation, the expected fidelity of each circuit on each available QPU. Then, a tunable scheduler uses these estimates to control the trade-off between execution fidelity and parallelism. Results show that this framework allows for approximating an exhaustive fidelity-based assignment, saving computational resources compared to a brute-force approach that compiles each circuit on every device.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a low-overhead, fidelity-aware scheduling framework for multi-QPU HPCQC platforms, using a Graph Neural Network to predict each circuit's expected execution fidelity on each QPU before compilation, enabling a tunable scheduler to balance fidelity against parallelism.
AI.motivation: HPCQC platforms expose multiple heterogeneous QPUs differing in size, topology, native gates, and noise. On noisy devices, errors accumulate rapidly along compiled circuits, so maximizing execution fidelity is critical. Fidelity depends on device-specific compilation, meaning the same high-level circuit yields different executables and expected fidelities across QPUs. However, evaluating fidelity on every device via brute-force compilation incurs prohibitive computational cost.
AI.method: A Graph Neural Network (GNN) is trained to estimate, prior to compilation, the expected fidelity of each circuit on each available QPU, avoiding per-device compilation. These estimates feed a tunable scheduler that trades off execution fidelity against parallelism.
AI.result: The framework approximates exhaustive fidelity-based assignment while saving computational resources relative to a brute-force approach that compiles every circuit on every device.
AI.conclusion: Fidelity-aware multi-QPU scheduling can be achieved at low overhead with GNN-based pre-compilation fidelity estimation, providing near-optimal assignment without exhaustive compilation.

title: Direct Cultivation of Entangled $|CS\rangle$ Magic States
summary: Magic-state cultivation has so far focused mainly on single-qubit non-Clifford resources. We develop a direct cultivation architecture for the entangled state $|CS\rangle=CS|++\rangle$. Two commuting Clifford involutions project onto four usable branches related by Pauli-frame updates. A minimal six-bit $[6,2,4]$ record protects the branch label against readout errors that map one valid record to another. Verified CAT$_7$ gadgets, Steane error detection, CZZ-based controlled checks, and immediate Steane-to-surface expansion form the complete factory. The decoder uses 263 operational detector bits, while 168 additional bits are withheld for later validation. Decoding proceeds through exact low-order resolution, a precomputed higher-order catalogue, and four-coset BP+OSD. Under the stated active-location stochastic-Pauli model, exact enumeration finds no accepted closed-boundary logical-failure mechanism through fault order two, while explicit order-three failure mechanisms exist. Finite-$p$ simulations quantify acceptance, residual syndromes, and decoder workload, and targeted sampling of order-three faults estimates the leading logical-error channels. Optimizing the direct $d=5\rightarrow13$ expansion reduces accepted-output operation count by approximately 35--37\%. We compare the two routes at the same binary logical-error rate. Direct CS remains cheaper in operation count at the two lower-noise benchmark points even when the three-$T$ route is given pre-existing output patches. The ordering reverses between $8\times10^{-4}$ and $9\times10^{-4}$. These results show that an entangled non-Clifford state can be cultivated directly with a protected branch record and an explicitly certified fault-order-three output channel.

AI.motivation: Magic-state cultivation has focused mainly on single-qubit non-Clifford resources; extending cultivation directly to entangled non-Clifford states is unexplored and could yield cost advantages over decomposing such states into single-qubit magic resources.
AI.method: Two commuting Clifford involutions project onto four usable branches related by Pauli-frame updates. A minimal six-bit [6,2,4] record protects the branch label against readout errors mapping one valid record to another. The factory uses verified CAT_7 gadgets, Steane error detection, CZZ-based controlled checks, and immediate Steane-to-surface expansion. The decoder uses 263 operational detector bits (with 168 additional bits withheld for later validation), proceeding via exact low-order resolution, a precomputed higher-order catalogue, and four-coset BP+OSD.

Finite-p simulations quantify acceptance, residual syndromes, and decoder workload; targeted order-three sampling estimates leading logical-error channels. Optimizing the direct d=5→13 expansion reduces accepted-output operation count by ~35–37%. At equal binary logical-error rate, direct CS is cheaper in operation count at the two lower-noise benchmark points even when the three-T route is given pre-existing output patches; the ordering reverses between 8×10⁻⁴ and 9×10⁻⁴.
AI.conclusion: An entangled non-Clifford state can be cultivated directly, using a protected branch record and an explicitly certified fault-order-three output channel, and this direct approach is operation-count competitive with (and at low noise superior to) the three-T route.

title: Coded Clifford Measurements for Multiqubit Magic-State Cultivation
summary: Magic-state cultivation suppresses errors by measuring logical Clifford symmetries and discarding inconsistent outcomes. For an entangled resource several branches are accepted, so the retained branch carries a multibit classical record whose corruption produces a logical-frame error. We show that this record layer is exactly a binary linear code. For any third-level Clifford-hierarchy unitary $U \in \mathcal{C}_3$, the branches $UZ(a)|+\rangle^{\otimes k}$ are resolved by commuting Hermitian Clifford observables $C(v) = UX(v)U^{\dagger}$, so a measurement schedule is a generator matrix and postselection on valid records gives $P_{\mathrm{wv}} = O(q^{d})$ at record distance $d$. A Plotkin bound then limits every binary record, linear or not. The physically realizable Clifford family already saturates it: at distance four, six logical measurements suffice for $|CS\rangle$ and seven for $|CCZ\rangle$, against eight and twelve for independent repetition. Restricting to fault-tolerantly measurable parities therefore costs nothing in record length. The saving survives compilation: in a native-CZZ-assisted Steane realization the $[6,2,4]$ CS schedule is the unique minimum-cost distance-four solution, reducing the cultivation core by 26.6\% in active locations, and exact state-vector simulation without a final ideal code-space projection confirms higher acceptance and roughly half the residual Steane-boundary weight. Coding thus reduces logical redundancy and compiled overhead together.

AI.tldr: The classical multibit record retained during magic-state cultivation is shown to be exactly a binary linear code; Plotkin bounds limit its distance, and the physically realizable Clifford measurement family already saturates the bound, reducing record length and compiled overhead.
AI.motivation: Magic-state cultivation suppresses errors by measuring logical Clifford symmetries and discarding inconsistent outcomes, but for entangled resources several branches are accepted, so the retained branch carries a multibit classical record whose corruption causes a logical-frame error. The paper aims to characterize this record layer and understand whether restricting to fault-tolerantly measurable parities costs anything in record length or compiled overhead.

For any third-level Clifford-hierarchy unitary U in C_3, the branches UZ(a)|+>^{⊗k} are resolved by commuting Hermitian Clifford observables C(v) = U X(v) U†, so a measurement schedule is a generator matrix; postselection on valid records yields P_wv = O(q^d) at record distance d. A Plotkin bound constrains every binary record, linear or not. They also compile the schedule into a native-CZZ-assisted Steane realization and perform exact state-vector simulation without a final ideal code-space projection.

In the native-CZZ-assisted Steane realization the [6,2,4] CS schedule is the unique minimum-cost distance-four solution, reducing the cultivation core by 26.6% in active locations; simulation confirms higher acceptance and roughly half the residual Steane-boundary weight.
AI.conclusion: Restricting to fault-tolerantly measurable parities costs nothing in record length, and the coding perspective reduces logical redundancy and compiled overhead together.

title: A Separation between Full-Rank PVM and Assumption-free Self-Testing
summary: We construct a nonlocal game that self-tests a maximally entangled qubit strategy among pure full-Schmidt-rank projective strategies, but admits an inequivalent optimum using one nonprojective measurement. This resolves a conjecture of Baptista et al. on imposing full rank and projectivity simultaneously. The construction combines CHSH with an auxiliary game $G$ that forces deterministic answers under these assumptions and admits a trine POVM optimum without them. We classify the optimal correlations of $G$ as a line segment parametrized by the tracial states of $\mathbb{C}\oplus M_2(\mathbb{C})$. Projectivity on the state support removes the matrix summand, whereas projective dilations with nonzero nonabort probability have a nontracial local state whose zero left ideal is not two-sided. Finally, a family in local dimension six shows that the full-rank PVM self-test is not robust.

AI.tldr: The paper constructs a nonlocal game that self-tests a maximally entangled qubit strategy among pure full-Schmidt-rank projective strategies, yet admits an inequivalent nonprojective optimum, resolving a conjecture by Baptista et al. It also shows the full-rank PVM self-test is not robust.
AI.motivation: Baptista et al. conjectured that full rank and projectivity can be imposed simultaneously in self-testing. The paper aims to resolve this conjecture by constructing a counterexample that separates these two conditions.
AI.method: The construction combines the CHSH game with an auxiliary game G that forces deterministic answers under full-rank projective assumptions but admits a trine POVM optimum otherwise. The optimal correlations of G are classified as a line segment parametrized by tracial states of C ⊕ M2(C).
AI.result: The game self-tests a maximally entangled qubit strategy among pure full-Schmidt-rank projective strategies but admits an inequivalent optimum using one nonprojective measurement. Projectivity on the state support removes the matrix summand; projective dilations with nonzero nonabort probability have a nontracial local state whose zero left ideal is not two-sided. A family in local dimension six demonstrates the full-rank PVM self-test is not robust.
AI.conclusion: The conjecture of Baptista et al. is resolved negatively: full rank and projectivity cannot be imposed simultaneously. Furthermore, the full-rank PVM self-test is shown to be non-robust in local dimension six.

title: One Relative Phase Orders Operational Thresholds of Noisy Bell Pairs
summary: Unlike the two-qubit entangled and CHSH-nonlocal sets, the steerable and Bell-nonlocal ones have no known general closed-form criterion. For any such operational ability whose failing states form a convex set closed under local unitaries, and for a Bell mixture with arbitrary noise, the $X$ part of the noise gives an upper bound on the definitive threshold, the Bell weight above which the mixture attains the ability. That bound is the tightest that the seven of the fifteen Pauli expectation values fixing the $X$ part can support. The same theorem shows that a state has the ability whenever its $X$ part does, so partial tomography of a state can certify its ability. When noise is of $X$ form, the mixture carries a relative phase between the noise and Bell coherences that cannot be gauged away by local unitaries, and it controls the threshold through interference. We prove a monotonicity law: the threshold is nondecreasing in this phase, whether or not a closed-form criterion for the ability exists.

AI.tldr: For steerable and Bell-nonlocal sets (which lack general closed-form criteria), the X-part of the noise in a Bell mixture yields an upper bound on the threshold Bell weight, and this threshold is monotonic in an ungaugable relative phase between noise and Bell coherences.
AI.motivation: Unlike two-qubit entangled and CHSH-nonlocal sets, steerable and Bell-nonlocal sets have no known general closed-form criterion, so practical tools for bounding and certifying these operational abilities are needed.
AI.method: For any operational ability whose failing states form a convex set closed under local unitaries, and for a Bell mixture with arbitrary noise, the authors analyze the X-part of the noise to bound the definitive threshold (the Bell weight above which the ability is attained). They exploit the seven of fifteen Pauli expectation values fixing the X-part and study a relative phase between noise and Bell coherences under local unitaries.
AI.result: The X-part of the noise gives an upper bound on the threshold, and this bound is the tightest supportable by the seven relevant Pauli expectation values. A state has the ability whenever its X-part does, enabling certification via partial tomography. When noise is of X form, the mixture carries a relative phase between noise and Bell coherences that cannot be gauged away and controls the threshold through interference.
AI.conclusion: The threshold is nondecreasing in the relative phase (a monotonicity law), holding whether or not a closed-form criterion for the ability exists.

title: Semi-device-independent quantum randomness certification in semiconductor spin-noise measurements
summary: Complex solid-state systems are promising platforms for scalable, high-bandwidth quantum random-number generation, yet certifying the quantum origin of their fluctuations remains difficult because the underlying microscopic dynamics are hard to model and validate. Here we demonstrate semi-device-independent quantum randomness certification from semiconductor spin noise, to our knowledge the first such certificate on any spin-noise source, without relying on a microscopic model of the spin system. The untrusted optical source is constrained by an experimentally tested mean-photon-number bound together with a declared analogue-range and per-sample clipping ceiling, while the trusted receiver is described as a calibrated, noisy, coarse-grained homodyne measurement. Using a semidefinite programme with rigorously controlled Fock-space truncation, we certify randomness that remains private against an adversary holding arbitrary quantum side information. Offline analysis yields certified entropy rates of $3.2$--$3.4$\,Gbit/s from a singly charged (In,Ga)As quantum-dot ensemble and $33$\,Mbit/s from $n$-GaAs in a spin-noise-matched detection mode. title: Quantum computational resources and validation protocols for a three-mode non-Gaussian trilinear Hamiltonian
summary: Non-Gaussian interactions are a key ingredient for achieving universality in continuous-variable quantum computation, yet their experimental characterization and the validation of their correct implementation remain challenging tasks. In this work, we focus on a three-mode non-Gaussian trilinear Hamiltonian that has recently been realized in superconducting microwave platforms, and present a comprehensive theoretical analysis of the computational resources it generates, together with experimentally accessible protocols to validate their presence. We systematically investigate its ability to generate two key resources for quantum computation: multipartite entanglement and Wigner negativity. In particular, using displaced-parity Bell tests, we demonstrate the generation of nonlocal states and thereby provide an operational certification of multipartite entanglement in the non-Gaussian states produced by the dynamics. We further quantify the Wigner logarithmic negativity and benchmark it against that of established non-Gaussian resource states. Building on this resource-based characterization, we introduce a measurement-efficient protocol for the experimental validation of the Hamiltonian implementation without requiring full reconstruction of the Wigner function. The protocol combines the measurement of zero-variance observables (nullifiers and stabilizers) with a limited number of targeted phase-space measurements, leading to a drastic reduction of the experimental overhead.

This motivates a systematic resource analysis and validation protocol for an experimentally realized non-Gaussian Hamiltonian.

They use displaced-parity Bell tests to certify nonlocality and multipartite entanglement, quantify Wigner logarithmic negativity and benchmark it against established non-Gaussian resource states. They also introduce a validation protocol combining measurements of zero-variance observables (nullifiers and stabilizers) with a limited number of targeted phase-space measurements, avoiding full Wigner function reconstruction.

title: Accelerating A*-Based Algorithms for Decoding Quantum Low-Density Parity-Check Codes
comment: Accepted for publication at IEEE PIMRC 2026
summary: Quantum low-density parity-check (QLDPC) codes represent a promising approach for error correction in quantum computing. The recently proposed Tesseract decoder uses the A* search algorithm that guarantees finding the most likely error pattern. However, practical implementations of Tesseract often involve an extremely large graph, and the inherently sequential nature of the search results in high computational overhead and long runtime. To improve decoding efficiency, we propose a two-stage decoding framework. First, a belief propagation (BP) decoder efficiently processes the syndrome. This step generates hard decisions (a binary error vector) and soft information (per-qubit confidence levels). In non-convergent BP cases, a gating mechanism examines the BP decoder's output to identify and filter out qubits with oscillating confidence values. In these cases, the refined output serves as input to Tesseract, which then attempts to identify and correct any residual errors. This hybrid approach leverages the high speed of BP decoding and delegates the more challenging decoding instances to Tesseract. Numerical results demonstrate a substantial reduction in overall decoding complexity while maintaining the logical error rate (LER) of the stand-alone Tesseract. Across all tested physical error rates, the proposed method achieves at least 5x reduction in the number of expanded nodes in the Tesseract, with a peak reduction of nearly 15x at a physical error rate of p = 0.05 for the [[126, 12, d < 11]] T1 code, and approximately 8.8x at p = 0.05 for the [[72, 12, 6]] bicycle bivariate (BB) code.

AI.tldr: A two-stage BP+Tesseract hybrid decoder reduces Tesseract's expanded-node count by 5x–15x while preserving the logical error rate of stand-alone Tesseract for QLDPC codes.
AI.motivation: Stand-alone Tesseract guarantees most-likely-error decoding but operates on an extremely large graph and is inherently sequential, causing high computational overhead and long runtime, limiting practical QLDPC decoding efficiency.
AI.method: A two-stage framework: BP decoding first processes the syndrome, producing hard decisions (binary error vector) and soft information (per-qubit confidences). In non-convergent cases, a gating mechanism filters out qubits with oscillating confidence values, and the refined output is passed to Tesseract to correct residual errors.

title: Haar-Bayesian Pure-State Prediction under Relative-Entropy Loss: Arbitrary-Effect Reduction and Global Optimality
summary: We study Haar-Bayesian prediction of one unmeasured copy of an unknown finite-dimensional pure quantum state after an arbitrary collective measurement on $n$ observed copies. Performance is evaluated by quantum relative entropy. For a fixed measurement, the Bayes predictive state is the posterior mean and the optimized conditional loss is its entropy. We then optimize the measurement over all POVMs on the symmetric subspace. For every nonzero positive effect $E$, the corresponding posterior predictive state is $μ_E=(I+nρ_E)/(n+d)$, where $ρ_E$ is the normalized one-particle marginal of $E$. Since a pure spectrum majorizes every density-operator spectrum, this identity gives an outcome-wise entropy lower bound. Coherent rank-one effects attain the bound, and their Haar orbit yields the highest-weight covariant POVM. Hence this POVM is globally Bayes optimal over all collective measurements and, by covariance, globally minimax. Its exact risk is $h_d((n+1)/(n+d))$, where $h_d(r)=-r\log r-(1-r)\log((1-r)/(d-1))$. The same arbitrary-effect reduction shows that the highest-weight POVM also maximizes the joint overlap between the latent pure state and its posterior predictive state, equivalently the mean posterior purity, with optimum $((n+1)^2+d-1)/(n+d)^2$.

AI.tldr: The paper determines the Bayes-optimal collective measurement for predicting one unmeasured copy of an unknown pure quantum state under Haar prior and relative-entropy loss, showing the highest-weight covariant POVM is globally optimal for both prediction and posterior purity.

While optimal measurements are known in some settings, the globally Bayes-optimal collective measurement under an operationally meaningful loss (quantum relative entropy) had not been fully characterized. The paper aims to close this gap for pure states.

The measurement is then optimized over all POVMs on the symmetric subspace. A key structural identity is derived for any nonzero positive effect E: the posterior predictive state is μ_E=(I+nρ_E)/(n+d), where ρ_E is the normalized one-particle marginal of E. Majorization and covariance arguments are used to identify optimal effects.

Coherent rank-one effects attain it, and their Haar orbit gives the highest-weight covariant POVM, proving global Bayes optimality over all collective measurements and, by covariance, global minimaxity. title: Why three? A two-level system with four mutually unbiased questions
summary: Two sharp yes/no questions are mutually unbiased if and only if their involutions anticommute. A set of unbiased questions is therefore a Clifford algebra, whose maximal size is odd, meaning four anticommuting questions typically imply a fifth: the two-level systems of real, complex and quaternionic quantum theory allow two, three and five questions, while four is skipped. Without this operator product restriction, a two-level system with four unbiased questions exists as the four-dimensional Bloch ball, the hyperbit. The single-system postulates that pick out the Jordan state spaces allow such a model, and only energy observability rules it out. We show what it lacks, and realise it inside two qubits: its Kirkwood-Dirac imaginary parts are hidden $\mathfrak{so}(4)$ generators, its composites allow entanglement but no interaction, and its 24-cell of states stays Spekkens preparation contextual down to depolarising strength $2/3$. In fermionic terms, the four questions are the Majorana operators of two modes while the fifth is parity: the four-question system is therefore the sector removed by parity superselection.

AI.tldr: The paper characterizes two-level systems defined by maximal sets of mutually unbiased yes/no questions, showing the quaternionic (five-question) case also admits a four-question "hyperbit" model that satisfies single-system postulates but is ruled out by energy observability, and realizes it inside two qubits as a parity-removed fermionic sector.
AI.motivation: Mutually unbiased questions correspond to anticommuting involutions, forcing a Clifford-algebraic structure whose maximal size is odd — so a fourth anticommuting question typically implies a fifth. This raises the question of whether a consistent two-level system with exactly four unbiased questions (skipping the quaternionic five) can exist, and what physical principles distinguish it from the real, complex, and quaternionic quantum theories.
AI.method: The authors map sets of mutually unbiased sharp yes/no questions to Clifford algebras of anticommuting involutions, exploit the odd maximal size of such algebras to identify the "missing fifth" question, and construct the four-question model as the four-dimensional Bloch ball (the hyperbit). They embed it within two qubits, analyze its Kirkwood-Dirac quasiprobability imaginary parts as hidden so(4) generators, examine its composite behavior (entanglement without interaction), and use the 24-cell of states to test Spekkens preparation contextuality under depolarising noise. The fermionic interpretation identifies the four questions as Majorana operators of two modes with parity as the fifth.
AI.result: The four-question hyperbit satisfies the single-system postulates that single out Jordan state spaces, with only energy observability excluding it. It is realizable inside two qubits: its Kirkwood-Dirac imaginary parts act as hidden so(4) generators, its composites support entanglement but no interaction, and its 24-cell of states remains Spekkens preparation contextual down to depolarising strength 2/3. In fermionic terms the four questions are the Majorana operators of two modes and the fifth is parity, making the four-question system exactly the sector removed by parity superselection.
AI.conclusion: The hyperbit is a viable but energy-unobservable two-level model that violates the operator-product restriction on mutually unbiased questions. It is precisely the parity-odd sector excluded by parity superselection, providing a fermionic characterization of why nature selects the quaternionic five-question (or lower) structures rather than the four-question alternative.

title: Loss-correcting fault-tolerant quantum computing architecture for neutral atoms
summary:
Neutral-atom arrays are a leading qubit technology for large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC). A dominant error source on this platform is qubit loss, which accrues with every operation and movement. The presence of loss undermines the promises of existing architectural work. Standard error correction targets stochastic Pauli errors and cannot correct loss, so most FTQC performance analyses are not directly compatible with it. Moreover, compilation and routing decisions, which strongly affect overall loss, are typically optimized against Pauli-error cost models and often remain loss-agnostic, potentially increasing exposure to the loss channel.
  In this work, we comprehensively model the effect of qubit loss on neutral-atom FTQC and develop a loss-tolerant transversal-gate architecture. We treat loss not as a predetermined error parameter but as a dynamic budget spent across a whole program, allowing us to control it by co-designing layout, compilation, and decoding. We target a physical implementation with no separate storage and entangling zones, eliminating the repeated SLM-AOD handoffs and long-distance shuttling that dominate loss in other layouts. We develop compiler optimizations that maximize gate parallelism while respecting the RF tone budget and AOD bandwidth constraints. Our work couples these with a loss-aware, delayed-erasure decoder and an end-to-end loss-aware magic state cultivation protocol. Overall, we improve accumulated loss per syndrome-extraction round by up to 2.15X against a zoned baseline and reduce logical error rates by over two orders of magnitude versus current architectures. Our framework also informs concrete device targets such as continuous reloading rates, AOD counts, and shuttling trajectory choices. We expect these insights to matter for system architects as neutral-atom hardware scales.
