title: In situ characterization of a photon-subtraction device via heralding counts and homodyne detection
summary: Photon subtraction is one of the most important techniques for generating non-Gaussian optical states and constitutes a key resource for quantum information processing and quantum metrology. The practical performance of a photon-subtraction device is primarily determined by the transmissivity of the beam splitter and the quantum efficiency of the heralding detector. Accurate knowledge of these parameters is therefore essential for assessing the quality of the generated non-classical states. In this work, we propose an experimentally feasible in situ scheme for the simultaneous estimation of these two parameters using only the measurement data produced during the operation of the device. Our protocol combines the click statistics of an on/off heralding detector with homodyne measurements performed on the transmitted mode of the beam splitter when fed by a displaced squeezed state. Within the framework of classical multi-parameter estimation theory, we derive the corresponding Fisher information matrix and investigate both joint and sequential estimation strategies. For simultaneous measurement of parameters, we evaluate the sloppiness of the underlying statistical model and analyze its dependence on the measured quadrature, probe photon number, squeezing fraction, beam splitter transmissivity, and detector efficiency. Our analysis proves that an appropriate choice of the homodyne quadrature substantially reduces parameter degeneracy and enables efficient simultaneous estimation. Furthermore, we show that the joint estimation strategy consistently provides a lower estimation bound than the sequential estimation approach over a broad range of experimentally relevant parameters.

AI.motivation: The practical performance of photon-subtraction devices—key resources for quantum information processing and metrology—depends critically on beam splitter transmissivity and heralding detector quantum efficiency. Accurate knowledge of these parameters is essential for assessing the quality of generated non-classical states, motivating an in situ estimation approach that relies only on data produced during device operation.

AI.conclusion: The proposed in situ scheme offers a practical route to simultaneous, precise characterization of photon-subtraction device parameters, with joint estimation preferred over sequential estimation for a wide range of experimental conditions.

title: Multiparameter quantum bounds for entanglement-assisted aperture synthesis
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures, 1 table. Submitted to Quantum Science and Technology
summary: Entanglement-assisted optical interferometry promises diffraction-limited imaging over baselines where light cannot be physically combined, but existing theory treats only a single visibility on one two-station baseline. This work formulates the multiparameter estimation problem for an M-station array imaging an extended scene. A reduction lemma shows that the multimode quantum Fisher information (QFI) equals the mean photon number times the QFI of a single delocalized photon, collapsing the problem to a finite-dimensional one. The local photon-number superselection rule (SSR) erases all phase information from the bare state, while shared entanglement restores a fraction f(r)=r/(1+r) of the QFI on a baseline supplied with r pairs -- a factor shown to be achievable, since the reduced two-mode state of any pair is exactly the two-station weak-thermal state. The QFI matrix and its mean Uhlmann curvature reveal numerically that a point source is measurement-compatible, whereas for every extended-source model examined it is incompatible, the Holevo bound exceeding the symmetric-logarithmic-derivative (SLD) bound by up to ~74%. An explicit collective receiver -- a global mode-sorting (quantum Fourier transform) measurement -- then attains a weighted variance within ~7% of the SLD bound and roughly an order of magnitude below an explicit pairwise receiver, and a noisy-resource advantage threshold gives the break-even baseline (~20 km for near-term parameters) beyond which repeater-distributed entanglement beats direct transmission. Finally, the optimal allocation of a finite entanglement budget is a convex program with a closed-form proportional (square-root-law) solution favoring low-visibility baselines. These results recast quantum aperture synthesis as collective multiparameter estimation and give concrete design targets, illustrated on the CHARA array.

The framework supplies concrete design targets—entanglement-restored QFI scaling, a near-optimal collective receiver, break-even baseline distances, and proportional entanglement allocation—demonstrated on the CHARA array.

title: The Sample Complexity of Quantum Entanglement Allocation
comment: 61 pages, 15 figures. Includes code and recorded data as ancillary files
summary: How many past requests are needed to decide which qubits should share entanglement? We show that the answer depends on the allocation choices created by the queries: a larger memory can require no more data. The memory stores a classical bit and answers requests through a fixed detector that preserves coherence within each measured sector. For independent commuting $X$- and $Z$-type Pauli queries, we characterize the full attainable prediction-contrast region and construct encodings that preserve the bit at every nonzero vertex. With sharp reports, a $d$-qubit path and groups of at most $k$ qubits have minimax excess error after $m$ requests proportional to $k^{-1}\min\{1,\sqrt{d\log(k+1)/m}\}$, uniformly for $2\leq k<d$. Connected biclique regions can grow without increasing sample demand when depth, region count and connections per region stay bounded. Preparation noise introduces a separate calibration requirement. We derive an exact tradeoff with extra fresh detector calls and transfer the learning law to structured transaction co-location. Population-risk experiments test the statistical predictions. We also compare encodings on a native 15-qubit device and learned partitions on public purchase baskets. The full chain wins on the device; frequency grouping outperforms basket search in the largest-capacity retail setting.

AI.motivation: The core motivation is to determine the sample complexity of deciding entanglement-sharing assignments among qubits from past requests, and to understand how memory size, query structure, and allocation choices affect the amount of data needed. A secondary motivation is to connect this quantum learning question to structured co-location and retail basket problems, testing whether the same learning laws transfer.

title: Quantum Barankin bounds beyond local unbiasedness: Analytic results for Gaussian states via a right-division framework
summary: We propose a quantum version of the Barankin bound as an alternative to the quantum Cramér-Rao bound for quantum parameter estimation. The quantum Barankin bound provides a lower bound on the mean squared error of estimators satisfying arbitrarily chosen bias constraints at arbitrarily chosen parameter points. In particular, unbiasedness over the entire parameter space can be imposed, yielding precision limits for globally unbiased quantum parameter estimation. In contrast to the recently derived quantum Barankin bound, which is based on a symmetric division superoperator, our bound is based on a nonsymmetric right-division superoperator. This formulation enables us to find analytic expressions for the Barankin matrix for Gaussian states, which allows for an efficient calculation of the bound. We demonstrate the usefulness of our results by applying them to various examples that exhibit the threshold effect in the few-shot regime, which is invisible to the standard quantum Cramér-Rao bound approach.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a quantum Barankin bound based on a nonsymmetric right-division superoperator, providing a tighter precision limit than the quantum Cramér-Rao bound for globally unbiased quantum parameter estimation, with analytic Gaussian-state expressions and demonstration of the threshold effect in the few-shot regime.
AI.motivation: The quantum Cramér-Rao bound, the standard tool for quantum parameter estimation, is limited: it relies on local unbiasedness and fails to capture the threshold effect in the few-shot regime. A bound capable of enforcing global unbiasedness constraints is needed.
AI.method: The authors formulate a quantum Barankin bound using a nonsymmetric right-division superoperator (in contrast to the existing symmetric-division-based quantum Barankin bound). This yields analytic expressions for the Barankin matrix for Gaussian states, enabling efficient bound computation.
AI.result: The bound gives a lower bound on the mean squared error of estimators under arbitrary bias constraints at arbitrary parameter points, including global unbiasedness. Analytical Barankin matrix expressions for Gaussian states make the bound computationally efficient. Examples reveal the threshold effect in the few-shot regime, which is invisible to the standard quantum Cramér-Rao bound.
AI.conclusion: The proposed quantum Barankin bound offers an alternative and more informative precision limit for quantum parameter estimation, capable of capturing global-unbiasedness constraints and threshold behavior missed by the quantum Cramér-Rao bound.

title: Unbounded degree overhead for Alice-conditioned quantum Bell certificates
summary: Requiring each sum-of-squares term to involve only one of Alice's measurement questions can impose an unbounded certification cost. In the simplest Bell scenario, we prove that no finite level of the Alice-conditioned NPA hierarchy contains all standard level-two Bell certificates. An explicit family of truncated positive functionals on the infinite dihedral group exceeds the tilted-CHSH quantum bound at every prescribed finite level, while a standard degree-two certificate is exact. A Fejer-weighted trace reduces positivity to a rank-one subtraction from a moving-average Gram matrix. The required conditioned level grows at least as $(2-α)^{-1/2}$ near the endpoint tilt. This bounds the degree of exact nice-SOS inputs to compiled-game soundness proofs. Consequently, no finite conditioned level certifies the entire optimal CHSH randomness tradeoff against quantum side information, although standard level two does. Away from the endpoint, we prove a sharp one-level cost throughout $α\in[13/10,3/2]$, using optimal-strategy kernels and exact Bernstein matrix positivity to certify a continuous interval. The results separate ordinary SOS degree from the resources keyed by single-question certificate structure.

AI.tldr: In the simplest Bell scenario, no finite level of the Alice-conditioned NPA hierarchy contains all standard level-two Bell certificates, so conditioning each SOS term on a single Alice question can incur unbounded certification cost.
AI.motivation: Restricting each sum-of-squares term to involve only one of Alice's measurement questions can impose unbounded certification cost, which bounds the degree of exact nice-SOS inputs usable in compiled-game soundness proofs and affects certification of the optimal CHSH randomness tradeoff.
AI.method: The authors construct an explicit family of truncated positive functionals on the infinite dihedral group violating the tilted-CHSH quantum bound at every prescribed finite Alice-conditioned NPA level, while remaining consistent with a standard degree-two certificate. A Fejer-weighted trace reduces positivity to a rank-one subtraction from a moving-average Gram matrix. They also use optimal-strategy kernels and exact Bernstein matrix positivity to certify a continuous interval away from the endpoint.
AI.result: The required conditioned level grows at least as (2-alpha)^{-1/2} near the endpoint tilt. No finite conditioned level certifies the entire optimal CHSH randomness tradeoff against quantum side information, though standard level two does. Away from the endpoint, a sharp one-level cost is proven throughout alpha in [13/10, 3/2].
AI.conclusion: Ordinary SOS degree and the resources keyed by single-question certificate structure are genuinely distinct, and Alice-conditioned hierarchies cannot match standard level-two certificates in general.

title: Finite-Particle Quantum Reduction of Thermodynamic Irreversibility
summary: Thermodynamics is useful because it lets us predict and control complex systems from a few accessible quantities when microscopic reconstruction is impractical. We ask whether this operational reduction can be less costly in a finite quantum system than in a matched classical one. We compare a few-boson Bose--Hubbard chain with its number-conserving classical-field counterpart under the same driving and the same coarse spatial record. The quantum system relaxes more in the observed particle distribution, yet the retained mean energy resolves more of the microscopic structure hidden by that record, leaving less information unusable and smaller entropy generation. We then close the process into a heat-engine cycle whose controls use only the measured mean energy and spatial record, not full state tomography; at matched thermal resources, the smaller entropy generation gives more work and higher efficiency. The advantage fades as the particle number grows toward the classical-field regime.

AI.tldr: A few-boson Bose-Hubbard chain is compared with its number-conserving classical-field counterpart under identical driving and coarse spatial observation, showing that the quantum system relaxes more in the observed distribution yet retains more microscopic structure in its mean energy, yielding less unusable information and smaller entropy generation, which translates into more work and higher efficiency in a mean-energy-controlled heat-engine cycle, with the advantage vanishing as particle number grows.
AI.motivation: Thermodynamics enables prediction and control of complex systems from a few accessible quantities when microscopic reconstruction is impractical. The paper asks whether this operational reduction—controlling a system via coarse observables—can be less costly in a finite quantum system than in a matched classical one.
AI.method: The authors compare a few-boson Bose-Hubbard chain with its number-conserving classical-field counterpart under the same driving and the same coarse spatial record. They quantify relaxation in the observed particle distribution, the information retained in the mean energy about microscopic structure hidden by that record, unusable information, and entropy generation. They then close the process into a heat-engine cycle controlled only by the measured mean energy and spatial record, not full state tomography, evaluated at matched thermal resources.
AI.result: The quantum system relaxes more in the observed particle distribution, yet the retained mean energy resolves more of the microscopic structure hidden by the coarse record, leaving less information unusable and producing smaller entropy generation. In the heat-engine cycle at matched thermal resources, this smaller entropy generation yields more work and higher efficiency. The advantage fades as the particle number grows toward the classical-field regime.
AI.conclusion: Operational thermodynamic reduction via coarse observables can be less costly in finite quantum systems than in matched classical counterparts, with quantum advantages in retained information, reduced entropy generation, and engine performance that diminish with increasing particle number approaching the classical-field limit.

title: Information capacity of quantum statistics: Fock-state tests of a discrete binary-sequence model on cloud photonic quantum processors
summary: Our central premise is that quantum mechanics may be the statistical limit of a more fundamental discrete theory: any such theory equips a physical system with a finite information capacity, and its departure from quantum statistics is controlled by how much of that capacity the system uses. We show that commercial cloud photonic quantum processors have reached the precision required to bound this capacity from below, using the binary-sequence model of Powers et al. as the concrete test theory: outcome probabilities arise from counting discrete sequences of length $n$, quantum mechanics is recovered as $n \to \infty$, and $n$ measures the information capacity of the register behind a prepared state. Photon Fock states $|1\rangle$, $|1,1\rangle$, heralded $|2\rangle$, and cascaded beam-splitter pairs are measured on programmable interferometers with dominant systematics determined in situ. The model's composition-consistent parametrization, singled out by requiring that rotations compose, recovers quantum mechanics with deviations $1.24/n$; a random-effects likelihood analysis calibrated by parametric bootstrap excludes all $n \le 100$: the information capacity of the register carrying the two-photon state, if finite, exceeds $10^2$. Cascaded beam splitters test the composition law directly: the data are split-invariant, excluding naive count composition at $8σ$ and confirming the interference-sign rule. Model-independently, curve-averaged deviations from the quantum partition law larger than $2.3\times10^{-2}$ are excluded at 95% CL, and the originally published linear parametrization is excluded outright. Because the compilation offset is frozen per circuit it is calibratable, opening the $10^{-3}$ floor ($n \sim 10^3$) to current hardware: cloud photonic processors are quantitative instruments for quantum foundations, and information capacity an experimentally boundable quantity.

AI.tldr: Commercial cloud photonic quantum processors can experimentally bound the finite information capacity of a fundamental discrete theory beneath quantum mechanics, excluding all capacities up to n ≤ 100 for two-photon states and reaching toward n ~ 10^3.
AI.motivation: The paper tests the premise that quantum mechanics is the statistical (n → ∞) limit of a more fundamental discrete theory with finite information capacity, using the binary-sequence model (Powers et al.). It aims to make information capacity an experimentally boundable quantity and to test the composition law directly, leveraging high-precision cloud photonic hardware.
AI.method: Photon Fock states |1⟩, |1,1⟩, heralded |2⟩, and cascaded beam-splitter pairs are measured on programmable interferometers, with dominant systematics characterized in situ. The model uses a composition-consistent parametrization (requiring rotations to compose), a random-effects likelihood analysis calibrated by parametric bootstrap, and model-independent curve-averaged tests of the quantum partition law and the interference-sign rule.
AI.result: The composition-consistent parametrization recovers quantum mechanics with deviations scaling as 1.24/n, and all n ≤ 100 are excluded, so the register's information capacity for the two-photon state, if finite, exceeds 10^2. Cascaded beam splitter data are split-invariant, excluding naive count composition at 8σ and confirming the interference-sign rule. Model-independently, curve-averaged deviations larger than 2.3×10^-2 from the quantum partition law are excluded at 95% CL, and the originally published linear parametrization is excluded outright.
AI.conclusion: Because the compilation offset is frozen per circuit it is calibratable, opening a 10^-3 floor (n ~ 10^3) accessible to current hardware. Cloud photonic processors thus serve as quantitative instruments for quantum foundations, and information capacity becomes an experimentally boundable quantity.

title: An analysis of iterative refinement for quantum linear system solvers
summary: We present and analyze an iterative refinement (IR) framework for improving the precision dependence of algorithms that combine a quantum linear system algorithm (QLSA) with quantum state tomography. Existing QLSAs achieve polylogarithmic dependence on the inverse error tolerance to prepare a quantum state encoding the solution, but extracting a classical description of such a state via tomography typically introduces a polynomial dependence on the target precision. To retain polylogarithmic dependence in the inverse error tolerance throughout the entire process, we develop an IR scheme that solves a sequence of related linear systems to progressively refine the solution while requiring only fixed-precision quantum subroutines, finally obtaining a classical description of a high-precision solution. We analyze the proposed framework under three input models: quantum-read/classical-write RAM (QRAM), linear combinations of unitaries (LCU), and sparse-access oracles. We evaluate the proposed scheme through numerical experiments on both quantum simulators and real quantum hardware. The results demonstrate that iterative refinement efficiently improves the precision of the solution and exhibits robustness to hardware noise.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an iterative refinement (IR) framework that preserves polylogarithmic dependence on inverse error tolerance when combining quantum linear system algorithms (QLSA) with quantum state tomography, achieving high-precision classical solutions using only fixed-precision quantum subroutines.
AI.motivation: QLSAs prepare quantum states encoding solutions with polylogarithmic dependence on inverse error tolerance, but extracting a classical description via tomography typically introduces polynomial dependence on target precision, breaking the desired scaling. The paper aims to retain polylogarithmic dependence throughout the whole process.
AI.method: The authors develop an iterative refinement scheme that solves a sequence of related linear systems to progressively refine the solution, requiring only fixed-precision quantum subroutines. They analyze the framework under three input models: quantum-read/classical-write RAM (QRAM), linear combinations of unitaries (LCU), and sparse-access oracles. Validation is done via numerical experiments on quantum simulators and real quantum hardware.
AI.result: Numerical experiments on both quantum simulators and real quantum hardware show that the iterative refinement scheme efficiently improves solution precision and is robust to hardware noise.
AI.conclusion: The proposed IR framework enables high-precision classical descriptions of QLSA solutions while maintaining polylogarithmic dependence on inverse error tolerance, and it performs effectively even under realistic hardware noise.

title: Solving wave propagation problems via geometric quantum state preparation on dispersion manifolds
summary: We present a quantum algorithm for solving partial differential equations through a linear-system formulation, focusing on wave propagation problems described by the discretized Helmholtz equation in frequency domain. Although quantum linear-system solvers offer exponential compression of the system degrees of freedom, their runtime complexity is generally governed by the condition number of the discretized operator. Exploiting the analytic structure of the differential operator can provide an alternative to explicit matrix inversion, as illustrated for the screened Poisson equation through an explicit quantum circuit. For the Helmholtz equation, however, the inverse operator becomes singular on the dispersion surface $k^2=ω^2/c^2$, rendering direct Fourier-space state-preparation methods exponentially inefficient. We address this challenge by directly preparing quantum states supported on the resonant manifold and encoding source locations through Fourier phases. The resulting algorithm eliminates the exponentially large overhead associated with post-selection on the resonant manifold, yielding a success probability that depends linearly on the number of sources and is independent of the computational domain size. More generally, our approach applies to hyperbolic differential equations whose Fourier-space solutions possess singular support on dispersion manifolds, recasting their solution as a problem of geometric quantum state preparation.

AI.tldr: A quantum algorithm solves the frequency-domain Helmholtz equation by directly preparing quantum states on the resonant (dispersion) manifold and encoding source locations via Fourier phases, avoiding exponentially inefficient post-selection and achieving success probability linear in the number of sources and independent of domain size.
AI.motivation: Quantum linear-system solvers give exponential compression of degrees of freedom for discretized PDEs, but their runtime is governed by the operator's condition number and by explicit matrix inversion. Exploiting the analytic structure of the differential operator (as done for the screened Poisson equation via an explicit quantum circuit) offers an alternative. For the Helmholtz equation, the inverse operator becomes singular on the dispersion surface k^2 = ω^2/c^2, which renders direct Fourier-space state-preparation methods exponentially inefficient.
AI.method: The authors avoid matrix inversion and direct Fourier-space state preparation by directly preparing quantum states supported on the resonant manifold, and encoding source locations through Fourier phases. This reframes the solution as geometric quantum state preparation on the dispersion manifold rather than post-selection.
AI.result: The algorithm eliminates the exponentially large overhead associated with post-selection on the resonant manifold. Its success probability scales linearly with the number of sources and is independent of the computational domain size. The approach generalizes to hyperbolic differential equations whose Fourier-space solutions possess singular support on dispersion manifolds.
AI.conclusion: Direct resonant-manifold state preparation with Fourier-phase source encoding provides an efficient quantum route to wave-propagation problems governed by the Helmholtz equation, and more broadly recasts solving hyperbolic PDEs with singular Fourier-space support as a problem of geometric quantum state preparation.

title: Programmable photonic state fusion via heralded storage of asynchronously generated resources
summary: Probabilistic photonic sources generate elementary states in different trials, whereas multiphoton protocols require them to interfere in common temporal modes. We propose a fusion protocol that overcomes this mismatch by successively loading independently heralded photonic states into active storage loops. Conditioning on vacuum in monitored dump modes selects events in which each newly generated state is transferred into the same circulating modes as the photons already stored, thereby removing its generation time label. Provided the two alternatives of each elementary state undergo the same loading transformation, the accumulated state is described by a product of programmable linear factors, allowing a target superposition to be constructed by polynomial factorization. Adjusting the storage loop coupling as the state grows substantially improves the loading efficiency, changing the faster-than-exponential penalty of fixed balanced couplers to exponential scaling. We apply the protocol to two-photon path--frequency states for photonic clock interferometry and estimate the detected rate including source waiting time and round-trip loss.

AI.tldr: A fusion protocol loads independently heralded photonic states into active storage loops, erasing generation-time labels and enabling programmable multiphoton superpositions via polynomial factorization, with coupling adjustment yielding exponential rather than faster-than-exponential loss scaling.
AI.motivation: Probabilistic photonic sources emit elementary states in different trials, but multiphoton protocols require these states to interfere in common temporal modes. This temporal-mode mismatch prevents direct scalability of heralded sources.
AI.method: Successively load independently heralded photonic states into active storage loops. Monitoring dump modes and conditioning on vacuum transfers each newly generated state into the same circulating modes as stored photons, removing the generation-time label. If both alternatives of each elementary state undergo identical loading transformations, the accumulated state factorizes into programmable linear factors, so a target superposition is built by polynomial factorization. Storage-loop coupling is tuned as the state grows.
AI.result: Adjusting the loop coupling as the state grows substantially improves loading efficiency, converting the faster-than-exponential penalty of fixed balanced couplers into exponential scaling. The protocol is applied to two-photon path-frequency states for photonic clock interferometry, with detected rate estimated including source waiting time and round-trip loss.
AI.conclusion: The proposed fusion protocol synchronizes probabilistic photonic sources into common temporal modes, enabling programmable multiphoton state construction with improved loss scaling, and is assessed for photonic clock interferometry.

title: Constant-depth global shadow estimation
summary: Reliable and scalable readout strategies are essential for quantum technologies. As quantum processors grow, extracting useful information must remain feasible without measurement circuits becoming a dominant bottleneck. Randomized measurements and classical shadows provide a powerful route, but global estimation is conventionally associated with highly random ensembles that require increasing circuit depth and hence substantial experimental overhead. In this work, we show that substantially less randomness suffices when the readout is meaningfully adapted to the quantities being estimated. We introduce shallow phase shadows, based on a sparse Clifford-IQP ensemble, and prove efficient global estimation of stabilizer-state fidelities despite the ensemble not forming an approximate relative-error design. On all-to-all architectures, the protocol admits a constant-depth implementation using mid-circuit measurements and classical feedforward, or logarithmic depth without auxiliary systems. The protocol requires only controlled-phase entangling gates and offers a tunable trade-off between circuit resources and estimation accuracy, making it particularly amenable to experimentally relevant architectures with long-range connectivity. Our results show that scalable quantum readout need not reproduce generic randomness: task-adapted randomization can enable substantially shallower global characterization protocols.

AI.tldr: Shallow phase shadows use a sparse Clifford-IQP ensemble to achieve efficient, scalable global estimation of stabilizer-state fidelities with only constant or logarithmic circuit depth, avoiding the expensive randomness of conventional classical shadows.
AI.motivation: As quantum processors scale, readout must not become a dominant bottleneck. Randomized measurements and classical shadows enable scalable readout, but global estimation conventionally relies on highly random ensembles requiring increasing circuit depth and substantial experimental overhead. The authors seek less randomness while retaining efficient global estimation.
AI.method: The paper introduces shallow phase shadows based on a sparse Clifford-IQP (instantaneous quantum polynomial) ensemble. The readout is task-adapted to the quantities estimated rather than reproducing generic randomness. The authors prove efficient global estimation of stabilizer-state fidelities even though the ensemble is not an approximate relative-error design. On all-to-all architectures, the protocol is implemented in constant depth using mid-circuit measurements and classical feedforward, or logarithmic depth without auxiliary systems, using only controlled-phase entangling gates.
AI.result: Efficient global estimation of stabilizer-state fidelities is proven possible with the sparse ensemble. The protocol achieves constant-depth implementation via mid-circuit measurements and feedforward, or logarithmic depth without ancillas, requiring only controlled-phase gates. It provides a tunable trade-off between circuit resources and estimation accuracy, suited to long-range-connectivity architectures.
AI.conclusion: Scalable quantum readout need not reproduce generic randomness. Task-adapted randomization enables substantially shallower global characterization protocols, making global estimation experimentally feasible without heavy circuit-depth overhead.

title: Faster Computation with the Generalized Laplacian Quantum Walk
comment: 6 pages, 3 figures; additional 7 pages of supplemental material
summary: Quantum walks are the quantum analogues of classical random walks or Markov chains. They are universal models of quantum computing, and they underpin a variety of quantum algorithms. We prove that a continuous-time quantum walk effected by a generalized Laplacian, which can arise in spin chains, can solve a computational problem more quickly than typical quantum walks governed by the standard Laplacian or adjacency matrix. This generalized Laplacian consists of the standard Laplacian plus a real-valued multiple of the degree matrix, and we prove that as the magnitude of the multiple of the degree matrix is increased, its corresponding quantum walk can search the complete bipartite graph with multiple marked vertices in time that approaches the optimal. This raises the potential for the generalized Laplacian quantum walk to be a useful method for developing additional faster quantum algorithms.

AI.tldr: A continuous-time quantum walk driven by a generalized Laplacian (standard Laplacian plus a real multiple of the degree matrix) outperforms standard walks, approaching optimal search time on complete bipartite graphs with multiple marked vertices as the multiple's magnitude increases.
AI.motivation: Quantum walks are universal models of quantum computing and underpin many quantum algorithms. Typical quantum walks are governed by the standard Laplacian or adjacency matrix, and the paper seeks a walk variant that can solve computational problems faster than these typical constructions, motivated by generalized Laplacians arising in spin chains.
AI.method: The authors analyze a continuous-time quantum walk effected by a generalized Laplacian, defined as the standard Laplacian plus a real-valued multiple of the degree matrix. They study its search behavior on the complete bipartite graph with multiple marked vertices, examining how the magnitude of the degree-matrix multiple affects the search time.
AI.result: As the magnitude of the multiple of the degree matrix is increased, the corresponding quantum walk searches the complete bipartite graph with multiple marked vertices in time that approaches the optimal, proving it can solve the problem more quickly than typical quantum walks governed by the standard Laplacian or adjacency matrix.
AI.conclusion: The generalized Laplacian quantum walk is shown to be faster than standard quantum walks, raising the potential for it to be a useful method for developing additional faster quantum algorithms.

title: Coherent advantage in the computational expressivity of excitonic networks
summary: The rising energy consumption of AI has generated interest in physical systems as alternative substrates for trainable computation. Recent experimental advances have enabled precise control over the couplings between molecular chromophores, which give rise to coherent excitation dynamics. Here, we study driven-dissipative excitonic networks as a computational platform, where the intersite couplings define the input and the steady state defines the output. We show that coherence enables computational expressivity to scale with network size, analogous to artificial neural networks. Both this scaling and the overall expressivity are suppressed by strong dephasing. Our work establishes coherence as a resource for expressive computation in nonequilibrium quantum systems.

AI.tldr: This work shows that driven-dissipative excitonic networks can act as a trainable computational substrate in which coherence enables computational expressivity to scale with network size, similar to artificial neural networks, while strong dephasing suppresses this scaling.
AI.motivation: Rising AI energy consumption motivates the search for physical systems as alternative computational substrates. Recent experimental control over molecular chromophore couplings, which produce coherent excitation dynamics, makes excitonic networks a promising candidate worth investigating.
AI.method: The authors study driven-dissipative excitonic networks as a computational platform, taking the intersite couplings as the input and the steady state as the output, and analyze how coherence, dephasing, and network size affect computational expressivity.
AI.result: Coherence allows computational expressivity to scale with network size in a manner analogous to artificial neural networks. This scaling, as well as the overall expressivity, is suppressed by strong dephasing.
AI.conclusion: The study establishes coherence as a resource for expressive computation in nonequilibrium quantum systems.

title: Symmetry structure dependent diagnostic of the Quantum Mpemba Effect
summary: Understanding symmetry restoration in isolated quantum many-body systems is an important problem in nonequilibrium many-body quantum physics. Recent studies have shown that the quantum Mpemba effect can be characterized through entanglement asymmetry, where states with stronger initial symmetry breaking restore symmetry faster. However, it remains unclear whether conventional energy-based measures, such as the trace distance, capture the same phenomenon. We investigate this question in closed spin-$1/2$ quantum systems with different symmetries by analyzing the dynamics of symmetry-breaking initial states. Combining numerical simulations with an analytical decomposition of the trace distance into symmetry-coherence and residual contributions, we identify the conditions under which trace distance tracks entanglement asymmetry and reproduces the Mpemba--like behavior observed in it. For charge symmetry, the residual contribution is negligible, making the trace distance effectively governed by symmetry-sector coherences. In contrast, for permutation symmetry, a significant residual contribution leads to qualitatively different relaxation dynamics. Our results establish when conventional energy-based diagnostics reliably capture symmetry-restoration dynamics and clarify the distinct physical information encoded by entanglement asymmetry and trace distance.

AI.tldr: This work examines whether the trace distance, an energy-based measure, can capture the quantum Mpemba effect in symmetry restoration, comparing it against entanglement asymmetry in closed spin-1/2 systems. It finds the trace distance tracks entanglement asymmetry only when the residual contribution is negligible, as in charge symmetry, but fails for permutation symmetry.
AI.motivation: Symmetry restoration in isolated quantum many-body systems is a key nonequilibrium problem. While the quantum Mpemba effect has been characterized via entanglement asymmetry, it remains unclear whether conventional energy-based measures like the trace distance capture the same phenomenon.
AI.method: The authors study closed spin-1/2 quantum systems with different symmetries, analyzing the dynamics of symmetry-breaking initial states. They combine numerical simulations with an analytical decomposition of the trace distance into symmetry-coherence and residual contributions.
AI.result: For charge symmetry, the residual contribution is negligible, so the trace distance is effectively governed by symmetry-sector coherences and tracks entanglement asymmetry, reproducing Mpemba-like behavior. For permutation symmetry, a significant residual contribution leads to qualitatively different relaxation dynamics.
AI.conclusion: The results establish when conventional energy-based diagnostics reliably capture symmetry-restoration dynamics and clarify the distinct physical information encoded by entanglement asymmetry versus trace distance.

title: Faster Quantum Monte Carlo Simulation by Random Compilation
summary: Quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) algorithms are among the most powerful classical methods for simulating quantum systems, yet their accuracy is often limited by the systematic errors in the approximations used, such as Trotterization. Here we introduce randomly compiled quantum Monte Carlo (RC-QMC) as a general framework that suppresses these systematic errors by averaging over a family of approximations rather than relying on a single fixed one. This strategy is grounded in the concept of randomized compiling from quantum computing, which suppresses errors by sampling over quantum gates, at essentially no additional computational cost. Consequently, our framework achieves a computational advantage over standard QMC methods when estimating a target state to a desired level of accuracy. We illustrate this advantage on two key Monte Carlo algorithms: (1) path integral quantum Monte Carlo for estimating thermal states, and (2) the quantum trajectories method for simulating open system dynamics. In aggregate, these results represent a cross-fertilization of quantum and classical algorithms, are readily generalizable to other QMC methods, and suggest wider applications in classical simulation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces randomly compiled quantum Monte Carlo (RC-QMC), a framework that averages over a family of approximations to suppress systematic errors (e.g., Trotterization), achieving a computational advantage over standard QMC.
AI.motivation: QMC algorithms are powerful classical tools for simulating quantum systems, but their accuracy is often limited by systematic errors arising from approximations such as Trotterization. A general approach to mitigate these errors is needed.
AI.method: RC-QMC applies the randomized compiling concept from quantum computing (sampling over quantum gates to suppress errors) to classical MC by averaging over a family of approximations instead of a single fixed one, at essentially no extra computational cost. It is illustrated on path integral QMC (thermal states) and the quantum trajectories method (open system dynamics).
AI.result: The framework suppresses systematic errors and attains a computational advantage over standard QMC when estimating a target state to a desired accuracy, demonstrated on path integral QMC and quantum trajectories.
AI.conclusion: RC-QMC represents a cross-fertilization of quantum and classical algorithms, is readily generalizable to other QMC methods, and suggests wider applications in classical simulation.

title: Information Causality Characterizes the Set of Quantum Correlations in the Simplest Bell Scenario
summary: Information causality (IC) was introduced as a physical principle constraining correlations in non-signaling theories. Whether it can recover the exact quantum correlation boundary, beyond Uffink's inequality, has remained an open question. Here, we combine its generalized formulation for correlated inputs with a new communication protocol to derive quantum Bell inequalities that exactly characterize the quantum correlations in the simplest bipartite Bell scenario, with two binary measurements. In particular, we derive the Tsirelson-Landau-Masanes criterion directly from IC. Thus, the generalized IC implies macroscopic locality, while we also present macroscopically local correlations that violate the generalized IC. This establishes that generalized IC is a strictly stronger principle in this scenario. Together with our earlier result that generalized IC implies a nontrivial communication complexity principle, these findings strengthen the role of information causality in explaining the limits of quantum nonlocality and provide a systematic route to deriving tighter bounds on the set of quantum correlations in more general Bell scenarios.

AI.tldr: Generalized information causality (IC), combined with a new communication protocol, yields quantum Bell inequalities that exactly characterize quantum correlations in the simplest bipartite Bell scenario with two binary measurements, deriving the Tsirelson-Landau-Masanes criterion directly from IC and showing generalized IC is strictly stronger than macroscopic locality.
AI.motivation: Information causality was proposed as a physical principle constraining correlations in non-signaling theories, but it remained an open question whether it can recover the exact quantum correlation boundary beyond Uffink's inequality. Resolving this would clarify the principle's power in explaining the limits of quantum nonlocality.
AI.method: The authors combine a generalized formulation of information causality for correlated inputs with a new communication protocol to derive quantum Bell inequalities, applying this framework to the simplest bipartite Bell scenario with two binary measurements.
AI.result: The derived inequalities exactly characterize quantum correlations in this scenario, and the Tsirelson-Landau-Masanes criterion is derived directly from IC. Generalized IC is shown to imply macroscopic locality, while some macroscopically local correlations violate generalized IC, establishing generalized IC as strictly stronger in this scenario. Combined with the earlier result that generalized IC implies a nontrivial communication complexity principle, these findings reinforce information causality's role.
AI.conclusion: Generalized information causality is a strictly stronger principle than macroscopic locality in the simplest bipartite Bell scenario and provides a systematic route to deriving tighter bounds on the set of quantum correlations in more general Bell scenarios.

title: Phase transitions in first-detection statistics of monitored long-range quantum walks
comment: 27 pages (7 main text + 20 supplemental material), 10 figures (3 figures + 7 supplemental figures)
summary: In a quantum walk, the first-detection return probability (FDRP) characterizes salient features, determining whether the quantum walk is transient or recurrent. We study the FDRP of quantum walks on a chain where the initial site is stroboscopically monitored by a detector and the walker performs long-range hopping between sites. We assume that the hopping strength decays with the distance $d$ as $d^{-α}$ and $α\geq 0$ and show that the power-law exponent $α$ critically determines the behavior of the FDRP. The value $α=1$ separates recurrent ($α<1$) from transient ($α>1$) quantum walks through a continuous phase transition in the total detection probability. For $α<1$, strong long-range hopping induces localization, resulting in unit total detection probability. Instead, for $α>1$ the long-range walk is transient and the return probability decays algebraically as a function of time as $t^{-β}$. The associated decay exponent $β$ features nonanalytic points as a function of $α$. Such singularities are not exclusively determined by the low-energy spectrum, but are caused by the interference between infrared and ultraviolet energy modes induced by projective measurements, signalling the emergence of critical behavior intrinsic to the non-unitary dynamics. These dynamics are solely controlled by tuning the long-range exponent $α$ and can thus be experimentally probed in atomic and molecular systems.

AI.tldr: The first-detection return probability of stroboscopically monitored quantum walks with long-range hopping decaying as d^{-α} undergoes a continuous phase transition at α=1, separating recurrent (α<1) from transient (α>1) regimes.
AI.motivation: Understanding whether a monitored quantum walk is transient or recurrent, and how long-range hopping controls this, requires characterizing the first-detection return probability.
AI.method: Analyze quantum walks on a chain where the initial site is periodically monitored by a detector and the walker performs power-law long-range hopping (strength ~ d^{-α}, α≥0).
AI.result: τhe exponent α critically governs the FDRP. α=1 separates recurrent (α<1, unit total detection probability via measurement-induced localization) from transient (α>1) behavior through a continuous phase transition. For α>1 the return probability decays algebraically as t^{-β}, with β exhibiting nonanalytic points versus α. These singularities arise from interference between infrared and ultraviolet energy modes induced by projective measurements, not solely from the low-energy spectrum.
AI.conclusion: Long-range exponent α solely controls the monitored walk's transience/recurrence and associated critical behavior, which can be experimentally probed in atomic and molecular systems.

title: Optimal Low-Rank Quantum State Tomography with Bounded-Sample Joint Measurements

AI.tldr: The paper establishes the optimal sample complexity for low-rank quantum state tomography with joint measurements on at most t samples, showing a Θ(dr/ε² · max{1, r/√t}) rate, with an adaptive lower bound and a matching nonadaptive Gaussian protocol.
AI.motivation: Prior work lacked tight sample-complexity characterizations for low-rank quantum state tomography when measurements can act jointly on multiple samples. Understanding exactly how much joint (entangled) measurements on at most t copies improve over single-sample measurements—and how many copies are needed to reach the unrestricted collective rate—was an open quantitative question.
AI.method: Lower bound: the support of a state with fixed uniform spectrum is varied, and the Fisher information trace of every joint measurement on t samples is bounded; the adaptive Fisher chain rule combined with the van Trees inequality yields the trace-norm lower bound (robust even to fully adaptive protocols). Upper bound: a nonadaptive tomography protocol based on a Gaussian joint measurement is constructed and analyzed using an explicit second-moment identity and a conditional Gaussian law outside the state's support, giving a rank-dependent error analysis.
AI.result: For sufficiently small ε, estimating an unknown rank-r state on C^d to trace-norm error ε with constant success probability requires and is achievable with Θ(dr/ε² · max{1, r/√t}) samples. Joint measurements on at most t samples improve single-sample algorithms by at most a factor √t, and jointly measuring order r² samples is necessary and sufficient to attain the unrestricted collective rate. The lower bound holds for adaptive protocols, while the matching upper bound is nonadaptive.
AI.conclusion: Joint measurements yield at most a √t speedup over single-sample measurement schemes, with the full collective advantage requiring order r² samples measured jointly. The tight adaptive lower bound and matching nonadaptive Gaussian protocol exactly characterize the optimal sample complexity of low-rank tomography under joint-measurement constraints.

title: Private communication via zero-private-capacity quantum channels
summary: Private communication over a noisy quantum channel requires reliable transmission to the receiver and secrecy from the environment. Whether two channels with zero private capacity can jointly enable private communication is a longstanding open problem in quantum information theory. Here we resolve this problem by exhibiting a four-level channel and a qubit erasure channel with half erasure probability, each with zero private capacity, whose joint use achieves more than 0.0001903 private bits per product use. The encoding gives the receiver a linear information gain with at most quadratic environmental leakage, enabling privacy through a fixed joint measurement and classical coding. This superactivation, impossible for independent classical memoryless wiretap channels, shows that a channel's private capacity alone does not determine its value for secure communication. The initial activation example was identified through interactions with large language models, and the result has been formalized in Lean 4.

AI.tldr: Two quantum channels each with zero private capacity—a four-level channel and a half-erasure qubit channel—jointly achieve positive private communication (>0.0001903 private bits per product use), demonstrating superactivation of private capacity.
AI.motivation: Private communication over noisy quantum channels requires both reliable transmission and secrecy. A longstanding open problem in quantum information theory asks whether two channels with zero private capacity can jointly enable private communication. Resolving this clarifies whether a channel's private capacity alone determines its value for secure communication.
AI.method: Exhibits a four-level channel and a qubit erasure channel with half erasure probability, each individually having zero private capacity. The encoding is designed to give the receiver a linear information gain while limiting environmental leakage to at most quadratic, enabling privacy via a fixed joint measurement and classical coding. Initial activation example identified via LLM interactions; result formalized in Lean 4.
AI.result: Joint use of the two zero-private-capacity channels achieves more than 0.0001903 private bits per product use. This superactivation is impossible for independent classical memoryless wiretap channels.
AI.conclusion: A channel's private capacity alone does not determine its value for secure communication, since two individually useless (zero private capacity) channels can be superactivated to enable private communication.

title: Noether Symmetries Generate Deterministic Energy-Harvesting Protocols
summary: We consider the general principles for when deterministic energy harvesting (DEH) is possible. DEH means absorbing energy from a fluctuating source without entropy being absorbed. We show that the symmetry structure of the source--harvester dynamics gives a general route beyond existing examples to identify DEH capable source states. Any continuous symmetry with a conserved Noether charge induces a source-side orbit of states that all implement the same deterministic harvester transition, provided the harvester boundary states are symmetry invariant. Consequently, one DEH capable source state with nonzero asymmetry between charge sectors can generate infinitely many simultaneously DEH capable source states. A Jaynes-Cummings model, a three-spin XX chain, and an SU(2) model illustrate the construction. We further extend Noether's theorem to generalised probabilistic theories and thereby generalise our main result. We further establish an asymmetry bound for harvesting, showing that source asymmetry cannot increase on average, while DEH saturates the bound exactly preserving asymmetry.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes general symmetry-based principles for when deterministic energy harvesting (DEH) is possible, showing that continuous symmetries with conserved Noether charges generate families of DEH-capable source states.
AI.motivation: DEH—absorbing energy from a fluctuating source without absorbing entropy—was known only through specific examples. The authors seek general principles that identify which source states permit DEH, moving beyond case-by-case demonstrations.
AI.method: The authors analyze the symmetry structure of source–harvester dynamics, proving that any continuous symmetry with a conserved Noether charge induces a source-side orbit of states implementing the same deterministic harvester transition, provided harvester boundary states are symmetry invariant. They further extend Noether's theorem to generalized probabilistic theories to generalize the main result, and derive an asymmetry bound for harvesting. Illustrative models include a Jaynes-Cummings model, a three-spin XX chain, and an SU(2) model.
AI.result: One DEH-capable source state with nonzero asymmetry between charge sectors generates infinitely many simultaneously DEH-capable source states. The asymmetry bound shows source asymmetry cannot increase on average, and DEH saturates the bound exactly while preserving asymmetry. The construction is verified in the three example models.
AI.conclusion: Symmetry provides a general, model-independent route to identifying DEH-capable source states and to generating large families of them via conserved Noether charges, with the theory extended to generalized probabilistic theories.
